title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
視其所以觀其所由察其所安人焉廋哉
人焉廋哉
馬應羲
同考試官教諭沈批〔是題作者體貼傳註不明文多牽滯簡明通暢僅見此篇茲錄〕
考試官訓導穆批〔甚得聖人觀人之意〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔典則〕
===
惟致審於觀人則人無難知矣蓋人不可以不
知也苟觀之不審何能得其情哉昔夫子之意
若曰人固未易知也而亦不難知也顧吾所以
觀之者何如耳故始則視履焉以考其行果爲
善歟抑爲惡歟自其顯者而別之也事雖善矣
而意之所從來未可知也吾則因事焉以逆其
志果爲己歟抑爲人歟又自其微者而觀之也
所由雖善然猶未知其心之所樂者果何如也
吾於是而加察焉或好德之無斁歟抑矯强於
punctuated:
第壹場
四書
「視其所以，觀其所由，察其所安，人焉廋哉？人焉廋哉？」
馬應羲
同考試官教諭沈批〔是題作者體貼傳註不明，文多牽滯，簡明通暢僅見此篇，茲錄。〕
考試官訓導穆批〔甚得聖人觀人之意。〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔典則。〕
惟致審於觀人，則人無難知矣。蓋人不可以不知也，苟觀之不審，何能得其情哉？昔夫子之意若曰：人固未易知也，而亦不難知也，顧吾所以觀之者何如耳。故始則視履焉，以考其行，果爲善歟？抑爲惡歟？自其顯者而別之也。事雖善矣，而意之所從來未可知也。吾則因事焉，以逆其志，果爲己歟？抑爲人歟？又自其微者而觀之也。所由雖善，然猶未知其心之所樂者果何如也。吾於是而加察焉，或好德之無斁歟？抑矯强於
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“Look at what a person does, observe the grounds from which he acts, and examine what he finds rest in. How can a person conceal himself? How can a person conceal himself?”
Ma Yingxi
Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor: “Those writing on this topic have failed to grasp the commentaries clearly, and their compositions are often strained and awkward. This essay alone is concise, clear, and fluent; it is therefore recorded here.”
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: “Very well captures the sage’s intention in observing people.”
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “Exemplary and proper.”
Only by exercising thorough scrutiny in observing people can one find them readily knowable. For one must know people; if one does not observe them carefully, how can one discover their true character? The Master’s meaning was as though he had said: People are indeed not easily known, yet neither are they difficult to know. It depends only on how I observe them. Thus, first I look at their conduct to assess their actions: are they doing good, or doing evil? This is to distinguish them by what is manifest. Though their deeds may be good, the source of their intentions cannot yet be known. I therefore use their deeds to discern their aims: are they acting for their own moral cultivation, or for the approval of others? This is further to observe them through what is subtle. Though the grounds of their actions may be good, one still does not know what it is that their hearts truly delight in. At this point I examine them still more closely: do they love virtue without tiring, or are they forcing themselves to act virtuously for …

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
一時歟蓋有以推其至隱而究其中心之誠否
也夫始焉而求之事繼焉而求之意又繼焉而
求之心既不因事而遺意又不因意而遺心則
夫顯微無間始終一德者可以知其爲君子否
則皆不免於小人之歸彼雖欲匿之也烏得而
匿之謂之曰人焉廋哉人焉廋哉信乎人莫能
欺而觀人之道盡矣抑考之夫子嘗曰吾以貌
觀人失之子羽以言觀人失之宰予他日又有
論篤色莊患不知人之訓則夫子於此一事蓋
===
屢言之豈非以人之不知則無以考德而省已
故詳於觀人者乃其所以自觀也歟
天地之道博也厚也高也明也悠也久也
段有成
同考試官教諭戴 批 平平寫出理致自在非淺學可到
考試官訓導穆 批 體認精切
考試官教諭鄭 批 善作中庸之義者
論造化本於誠而各極其盛焉蓋誠體物而不
punctuated:
一時歟？蓋有以推其至隱，而究其中心之誠否也。夫始焉而求之事，繼焉而求之意，又繼焉而求之心，既不因事而遺意，又不因意而遺心，則夫顯微無間、始終一德者，可以知其爲君子；否則皆不免於小人之歸。彼雖欲匿之也，烏得而匿之？謂之曰：「人焉廋哉！人焉廋哉！」信乎人莫能欺，而觀人之道盡矣。抑考之，夫子嘗曰：「吾以貌觀人，失之子羽；以言觀人，失之宰予。」他日又有「論篤色莊」患不知人之訓，則夫子於此一事蓋屢言之。豈非以人之不知，則無以考德而省已，故詳於觀人者，乃其所以自觀也歟？

天地之道，博也，厚也，高也，明也，悠也，久也。
段有成
同考試官教諭戴批：平平寫出，理致自在，非淺學可到。
考試官訓導穆批：體認精切。
考試官教諭鄭批：善作中庸之義者。

論造化本於誠，而各極其盛焉。蓋誠體物而不
translation_en:
…for a moment? This enables one to probe what is most hidden and determine whether a person is sincere at heart. First one seeks to understand his deeds, then his intentions, and then his heart. If one neither overlooks intentions on account of deeds nor overlooks the heart on account of intentions, one can recognize as a gentleman someone whose manifest and hidden aspects are consistent and whose virtue remains the same from beginning to end. Otherwise, he cannot escape being classed as a petty man. Though he wishes to conceal himself, how could he do so? Hence the saying: “How can a person hide? How can a person hide?” Truly, no one can deceive us, and the method of observing people is fully set forth. Yet consider also that the Master once said: “When I judged people by their appearance, I was mistaken about Ziyu; when I judged people by their words, I was mistaken about Zai Yu.” On another occasion, he warned of the difficulty of knowing people whose “discourse is earnest and countenance solemn.” Thus the Master spoke repeatedly about this matter. Was this not because, without knowing others, one has no means to assess virtue and examine oneself, so that careful observation of others is precisely the means of observing oneself?

“The Way of Heaven and Earth is broad, deep, high, bright, far-reaching, and enduring.”
Duan Youcheng
Associate Examiner Dai, Instructor, comments: “Written with unassuming simplicity, its meaning and principles emerge naturally; this is beyond the reach of shallow learning.”
Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor, comments: “His understanding is refined and exact.”
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “One skilled in composing essays on the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean.”

I submit that the creative transformations of Heaven and Earth are rooted in sincerity, and that each thereby attains its fullest flourishing. For sincerity constitutes things and does not…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
遺也孰謂天地之極盛不本於誠之所爲乎宜
中庸言之以明至誠無息之功用也且夫天地
之道誠而已矣語其理則無二言其運則不息
故其爲道雖無聲臭之可名要之一誠實爲造
化之根柢則其盛何如哉自地言之人但見其
隤然而已而不知其質之凝也一氣之所磅礴
求之愈遠而莫知其畔岸測之愈深而莫知其
底止是何其博厚乎蓋坤道之盛所以載物者
在是矣自天言之人但見其確然而已而不知
===
其象之垂也一氣之所充周穹窿冲漠上徹於
無際宣朗昭融旁燭於無疆是何其高明乎蓋
乾道之盛所以覆物者在是矣然博厚高明又
豈局於淺近而法象於一時哉殆見地位乎下
而安貞不遷天位乎上而運轉有恒推之於前
而不見其始引之於後而莫知其終蓋一氣之
所貫徹所謂博厚高明者又極於悠乆而有以
成乎物矣向使非誠則造化亦幾乎息矣烏能
各極其盛之若是哉即此則至誠之功用可推
punctuated: 遺也，孰謂天地之極盛不本於誠之所爲乎？宜《中庸》言之，以明至誠無息之功用也。且夫天地之道，誠而已矣。語其理則無二，言其運則不息。故其爲道，雖無聲臭之可名，要之一誠，實爲造化之根柢，則其盛何如哉？自地言之，人但見其隤然而已，而不知其質之凝也，一氣之所磅礴。求之愈遠而莫知其畔岸，測之愈深而莫知其底止，是何其博厚乎！蓋坤道之盛，所以載物者在是矣。自天言之，人但見其確然而已，而不知其象之垂也，一氣之所充周。穹窿冲漠，上徹於無際；宣朗昭融，旁燭於無疆，是何其高明乎！蓋乾道之盛，所以覆物者在是矣。然博厚高明，又豈局於淺近而法象於一時哉？殆見地位乎下而安貞不遷，天位乎上而運轉有恒。推之於前而不見其始，引之於後而莫知其終。蓋一氣之所貫徹，所謂博厚高明者，又極於悠乆而有以成乎物矣。向使非誠，則造化亦幾乎息矣，烏能各極其盛之若是哉？即此則至誠之功用可推
translation_en:
…leaves nothing out. Who could say that the supreme fullness of Heaven and Earth is not grounded in what sincerity accomplishes? Fittingly, the Doctrine of the Mean speaks of this to illuminate the efficacy of utmost sincerity, which never ceases. Now, the Way of Heaven and Earth is simply sincerity. In its principle it is undivided; in its operation it is unceasing. Thus, although this Way has neither sound nor scent by which it might be named, sincerity alone is truly the foundation of creation and transformation. How great, then, is its fullness!

Speaking of Earth, people see only its yielding repose, without knowing that its substance is the condensation of the single vital force, spreading expansively. The farther one pursues it, the less one can discern its boundaries; the deeper one measures it, the less one can discern its bottom. How broad and deep it is! Herein lies the fullness of the Way of Kun, the Receptive, by which it bears all things. Speaking of Heaven, people see only its firmness, without knowing that its manifest forms are filled throughout by the single vital force. Vaulted high, empty and still, it extends upward without limit; clear and luminous, it shines in every direction without bounds. How lofty and bright it is! Herein lies the fullness of the Way of Qian, the Creative, by which it covers all things.

Yet could such breadth, depth, loftiness, and brightness be confined to what is shallow and near, manifesting their patterns and forms only for a time? We see Earth situated below, resting steadfastly without shifting, and Heaven situated above, revolving with constancy. Trace them backward and their beginning cannot be seen; extend them forward and their end cannot be known. Since the single vital force permeates them throughout, their breadth, depth, loftiness, and brightness also attain the utmost duration and persistence, thereby bringing things to completion. Were it not for sincerity, creation and transformation would all but cease. How could Heaven and Earth each attain such fullness? From this, the efficacy of utmost sincerity may be inferred…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
矣大抵天地之道皆實理聖人之德皆實心其
致用一也然而位育之効必本於中和之致而
彌綸參賛非盡性者不能也是聖人有功於天
地豈特同之而已哉然則未至於聖者當何如
亦曰思誠而已矣
以德服人者中心悅而誠服也如七十子
之服孔子也
楊茂時
同考試官訓導許批題本平易作者類騁浮辭前後
纒繞惟此篇見理頗明遣語簡當亦滇士之難得者
考試官訓導穆批平實
考試官教諭鄭批不事雕琢而意已足
===
大賢論王道得人之應而深著其出於誠也蓋
人之相感者心也王道誠矣則人之應之也又
豈有不誠者哉宜孟子以聖德之感人者形容
之也且其意若曰惟道爲能公天下而無私惟
誠可以通天下而無間蓋甞觀諸王者德蘊諸
己必達之於政而民之沐其休澤者咸尊之爲
punctuated:
矣。大抵天地之道皆實理，聖人之德皆實心，其致用一也。然而位育之効，必本於中和之致，而彌綸參賛，非盡性者不能也。是聖人有功於天地，豈特同之而已哉？然則未至於聖者當何如？亦曰思誠而已矣。
以德服人者，中心悅而誠服也，如七十子之服孔子也。
楊茂時
同考試官訓導許批：題本平易，作者類騁浮辭，前後纒繞。惟此篇見理頗明，遣語簡當，亦滇士之難得者。
考試官訓導穆批：平實。
考試官教諭鄭批：不事雕琢而意已足。
大賢論王道得人之應，而深著其出於誠也。蓋人之相感者，心也。王道誠矣，則人之應之也，又豈有不誠者哉？宜孟子以聖德之感人者形容之也。且其意若曰：惟道爲能公天下而無私，惟誠可以通天下而無間。蓋甞觀諸王者，德蘊諸己，必達之於政，而民之沐其休澤者，咸尊之爲
translation_en:
… indeed. In general, the Way of Heaven and Earth consists entirely in true principle, and the virtue of the sage consists entirely in a sincere heart; in their operation, they are one. Yet the result whereby Heaven and Earth take their proper places and all things receive nurture must rest upon equilibrium and harmony brought to their utmost. Only one who fully realizes his nature can encompass the workings of Heaven and Earth and assist their transforming and nourishing activity. Thus the sage contributes to Heaven and Earth: how could he merely be their equal? What, then, should those who have not yet attained sagehood do? Simply strive for sincerity.
“Those who win submission through virtue gain submission that comes sincerely from delight within the heart, as the seventy disciples submitted to Kongzi.”
Yang Maoshi
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Assistant Instructor: The topic is straightforward, but writers generally indulge in empty phrases, entangling their arguments from beginning to end. This essay alone shows a fairly clear understanding of principle and employs concise, apt language. Such work is rare even among the scholars of Yunnan.
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: Plain and substantial.
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Without elaborate embellishment, the meaning is fully expressed.
The great worthy discusses the response that the Kingly Way wins from people and makes especially clear that it springs from sincerity. For it is through the heart that people move one another. If the Kingly Way is sincere, how could people’s response to it be anything but sincere? Fittingly, Mengzi illustrates this through the way a sage’s virtue moves people. His meaning is something like this: only the Way can treat all under Heaven impartially, without selfishness; only sincerity can establish communion throughout all under Heaven without obstruction. Consider the true kings: the virtue stored within themselves must find expression in their government, and the people who bask in their beneficent blessings all honor them as …

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
元后政非徒法必本之於心而民之蒙其惠利
者咸戴之爲父母非强之也上以誠感則下以
誠應媚茲之念盖有維諸中而不可解者非要
之也上旣好仁則下必好義親比之意盖實由
於衷而不能已也然果何所似哉譬如七十子
之於孔子仰道德之高厚終身以之爲依歸荷
恩義之綢繆無往不隆其師事陳蔡之厄困矣
猶相從而不忍舍匡人之圍急矣雖冒險在所
不辭盖其感之者皆至德而服之者皆眞心區
===
區尊禮之間不足言矣王者思服之民亦何以
異於是哉噫此王道之所以爲大也歟抑論之
三代以降王道之不行也久矣漢文之天資近
道然亦雜於黃老願治如唐太宗猶未免有假
之之意然皆足以致一代之治况純用德教者
其效當何如耶至是然後知孟子之言爲有驗
彼謂王道不可行者特未之思耳
易
九二見龍在田利見大人
punctuated:
元后。政非徒法，必本之於心，而民之蒙其惠利者咸戴之爲父母，非强之也。上以誠感，則下以誠應，媚茲之念盖有維諸中而不可解者，非要之也。上旣好仁，則下必好義，親比之意盖實由於衷而不能已也。然果何所似哉？譬如七十子之於孔子，仰道德之高厚，終身以之爲依歸；荷恩義之綢繆，無往不隆其師事。陳蔡之厄困矣，猶相從而不忍舍；匡人之圍急矣，雖冒險在所不辭。盖其感之者皆至德，而服之者皆眞心，區區尊禮之間不足言矣。王者思服之民，亦何以異於是哉？噫！此王道之所以爲大也歟！抑論之，三代以降，王道之不行也久矣。漢文之天資近道，然亦雜於黃老；願治如唐太宗，猶未免有假之之意。然皆足以致一代之治，况純用德教者，其效當何如耶？至是然後知孟子之言爲有驗。彼謂王道不可行者，特未之思耳。

易

九二，見龍在田，利見大人。
translation_en:
…as their sovereign. Government is not merely a matter of laws: it must be rooted in the heart. The people who receive its benefits all revere the ruler as their father and mother, without being compelled to do so. When those above move others through sincerity, those below respond with sincerity. Their affection for him is bound within their hearts and cannot be undone; it is not exacted from them. When those above cherish benevolence, those below will surely cherish righteousness. Their desire for closeness truly springs from within and cannot be restrained. What, then, does this resemble? It is like the seventy disciples’ relationship to Confucius. Looking up to the height and depth of his moral virtue, they relied upon him throughout their lives. Receiving his closely entwined kindness and righteousness, wherever they went they served him with the utmost reverence as their teacher. The ordeal in Chen and Cai brought severe hardship, yet they continued to follow him and could not bear to leave. The encirclement by the people of Kuang brought urgent danger, yet they did not shrink from risking themselves. What moved them was consummate virtue, and their submission came from true hearts; mere outward observances of respect scarcely merit mention. How could the people who yearn for and submit to a true king differ from this? Ah! Is this not what makes the Kingly Way so great?

To consider the matter further: since the Three Dynasties, the Kingly Way has long gone unpracticed. Emperor Wen of Han was naturally close to the Way, yet his practice was also mixed with the teachings of Huang-Lao. Even someone as eager for good government as Emperor Taizong of Tang could not escape an intention to borrow the semblance of virtue. Yet both were able to bring good government to their respective ages. How much greater, then, should the results be for one who relies entirely on moral instruction? Only at this point do we recognize that Mencius’s words have been borne out. Those who say that the Kingly Way cannot be practiced have simply failed to think it through.

Book of Changes

Nine in the second place: A dragon appears in the field. It is beneficial to see the great man.

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
馬應羲
同考試官教諭沈批九二備龍德而當正中之時者
也作者措辭多類九五殊失本旨此作得之
考試官訓導穆批理明辭暢
考試官教諭鄭批發揮象占明當可取
聖人於乾之九二擬以顯德之象示以仰德之
占盖九二備龍德於已為人所利見者也聖人
擬象示占之意良有以哉昔伏羲畫乾之卦爻
至九二周公繫辭盖謂非德不足以善世非時
===
不足以顯德九二君子備剛健中正之德當出
潜離隱之時位雖在下也然盛德至善之懿不
俟教令而輝光所被自有舍舊從新之化時雖
未遇也然天德王道之妙無假言說而心迹所
及自有遷善敏德之休是猶神龍起蟄霖雨將
於此而普施也龍見于田膏澤將於此而廣布
也其象如此占者值之當何如哉必以是大人
者偉然斯世之望于焉尊德樂道而趨承之不
違卓乎萬民之瞻于焉致敬盡禮而親比之恐
punctuated:
馬應羲。
同考試官教諭沈批：九二備龍德而當正中之時者也。作者措辭多類九五，殊失本旨，此作得之。
考試官訓導穆批：理明辭暢。
考試官教諭鄭批：發揮象占，明當可取。
聖人於乾之九二，擬以顯德之象，示以仰德之占。盖九二備龍德於已，為人所利見者也。聖人擬象示占之意，良有以哉！昔伏羲畫乾之卦爻，至九二，周公繫辭，盖謂非德不足以善世，非時不足以顯德。九二君子備剛健中正之德，當出潜離隱之時。位雖在下也，然盛德至善之懿，不俟教令，而輝光所被，自有舍舊從新之化；時雖未遇也，然天德王道之妙，無假言說，而心迹所及，自有遷善敏德之休。是猶神龍起蟄，霖雨將於此而普施也；龍見于田，膏澤將於此而廣布也。其象如此，占者值之，當何如哉？必以是大人者，偉然斯世之望，于焉尊德樂道，而趨承之不違；卓乎萬民之瞻，于焉致敬盡禮，而親比之恐
translation_en:
Ma Yingxi.
Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor, comments: “Nine in the second place possesses the dragon’s virtue and occupies a time of proper centrality. Writers often phrase their answers as though discussing nine in the fifth place, gravely missing the original meaning. This answer captures it.”
Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor, comments: “The reasoning is clear and the language flows freely.”
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: “The exposition of the image and the divinatory pronouncement is clear, apt, and worthy of acceptance.”
For nine in the second place of Qian, the sage devised an image of manifest virtue and presented a divinatory pronouncement about looking up to virtue. For nine in the second place possesses the dragon’s virtue within himself [?] and is one whom it benefits others to see. The sage indeed had good reason for devising this image and presenting this pronouncement! Long ago, Fuxi drew the hexagram Qian and its lines. For nine in the second place, the Duke of Zhou appended a statement, meaning that without virtue one cannot make the world good, and without the proper time one cannot manifest virtue.
The gentleman represented by nine in the second place possesses the virtues of firmness, vigor, centrality, and correctness, and has reached the time to emerge from concealment and leave seclusion. Although his position is low, the excellence of his abundant virtue and supreme goodness brings transformation wherever its radiance reaches: people abandon the old and follow the new without waiting for instruction or commands. Although he has not yet encountered his opportunity, the subtle workings of his heavenly virtue and kingly Way bring the blessings of turning toward goodness and diligently cultivating virtue wherever his intentions and conduct reach, without recourse to verbal explanation. This is like a divine dragon awakening from hibernation, from which timely rain will spread everywhere; the dragon appears in the fields, from which nourishing moisture will be widely bestowed.
Such is the image. What should a diviner do upon encountering it? He must regard this great man as the towering hope of the age, honor his virtue and delight in his Way, and hasten to attend him without departing from him. As this man stands preeminent, the object of all the people’s regard, the diviner must show reverence, fulfill every courtesy, and draw close to him, fearing…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
後上焉者寤寐臣隣而克勤乎下交之儀則謀
猷相資大業以之而成矣下焉者仰止神聖而
聿興乎快覩之念則矜式所在習俗以之而美
矣何利如之占者若有見龍之德則當利見九
五在上之大人也周公擬象示占之意精矣哉
抑因是而求之大舜矣歷山之耕河濱之陶身
雖側微而濬哲文明温恭允塞其德固已昭著
於天下而升聞于帝堯矣當時耕者讓畔器不
苦窳以至主祭而神享主事而民安澤及於物
===
豈非天下利見之時乎是必有如是聖人之德
而後可以當是爻之用
履和而至謙尊而光復小而辨於物恒雜
而不厭損先難而後易益長裕而不設
困窮而通井居其所而遷巽稱而隱
劉舉良
同考試官教諭沈批講九德抑揚處辭不費而理已
具可以占所養矣
考試官訓導穆批文有變態自超衆作
punctuated:
後。上焉者，寤寐臣隣，而克勤乎下交之儀，則謀猷相資，大業以之而成矣；下焉者，仰止神聖，而聿興乎快覩之念，則矜式所在，習俗以之而美矣。何利如之？占者若有見龍之德，則當利見九五在上之大人也。周公擬象示占之意，精矣哉！抑因是而求之，大舜矣。歷山之耕，河濱之陶，身雖側微，而濬哲文明，温恭允塞，其德固已昭著於天下，而升聞于帝堯矣。當時耕者讓畔，器不苦窳，以至主祭而神享，主事而民安，澤及於物，豈非天下利見之時乎？是必有如是聖人之德，而後可以當是爻之用。

履和而至，謙尊而光，復小而辨於物，恒雜而不厭，損先難而後易，益長裕而不設，困窮而通，井居其所而遷，巽稱而隱。

劉舉良。

同考試官教諭沈批：講九德抑揚處，辭不費而理已具，可以占所養矣。

考試官訓導穆批：文有變態，自超衆作。
translation_en:
…fall behind. If those above yearn, waking and sleeping, for ministers to stand beside them, and diligently observe the proprieties of associating with those below, their plans and counsels will complement one another, and great undertakings will thereby be accomplished. If those below look up to the sage and eagerly wish to behold him, they will have a model to emulate, and prevailing customs will thereby improve. What benefit could equal this? If the diviner possesses the virtue of the dragon appearing in the field, then it is fitting for him to seek an audience with the great man above, represented by the nine in the fifth place. How subtle was the Duke of Zhou’s intention in framing the image and indicating its divinatory meaning!

If we pursue this further through an example, we find the great Shun. When he farmed at Lishan and made pottery on the riverbank, his station was humble and obscure. Yet he was profound and wise, cultivated and discerning, gentle and reverent, sincere and trustworthy. His virtue had already become manifest throughout the world, and its fame had reached Emperor Yao. In those days, cultivators yielded field boundaries to one another, and pottery was free of flaws. Eventually, when he presided over sacrifices, the spirits accepted the offerings; when he directed affairs, the people enjoyed peace. His beneficence extended to all things. Was this not a time when all under Heaven benefited from seeing him? Only one possessing such sagely virtue can fulfill the function of this line.

Treading (Lü) is harmonious and reaches its goal; Modesty (Qian) is honored and radiant; Return (Fu) is small yet distinguishes among things; Constancy (Heng) encounters complexity without weariness; Decrease (Sun) brings difficulty first and ease afterward; Increase (Yi) brings enduring abundance without contrivance; Constraint (Kun) is hemmed in yet finds passage; The Well (Jing) remains in its place yet brings movement; The Gentle (Xun) fits circumstances yet remains hidden.

Liu Juliang.

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Instructor: “In explaining the contrasting aspects of the nine virtues, the wording is economical, yet the principles are fully present. From this one can judge the author’s cultivation.”

Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: “The composition displays varied forms and naturally surpasses the other works.”

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭鄭批〔簡潔粹徹得易本旨〕
大傳論九卦之德之妙以明處憂患之道也夫
易卦之德周天下之用也即九卦而德皆不偏
焉其於處憂患也何有昔吾夫子大傳論九卦
之德而再陳之若謂易非聖人不能作德非諸
卦不能備然或涉於一偏未免滯於日用是故
禮者順人情而非强世若和矣然品節詳明事
理精當而實爲至焉謙者德欲盛而禮欲恭若
卑矣然天道所益人道所好而尊且光焉復以
===
一陽生於羣陰之下何其小也然善端既復欲
不能間矣豈以小而無辨乎恒以一身混於紛
華之中何其雜也然常德在我久而不變矣豈
以雜而有厭乎至若懲忿窒慾以脩身損先焉
難從事既久則無忿可懲無慾可窒也何易如
之遷善改過以長善益實自裕究而言之則善
所本有過所本無也何設之有窮與通異困爲
柔揜不能以自振者但實德既脩心無怨尤無
入而不自得矣靜與動反井居其所不能以自
punctuated:
考試官教諭鄭批〔簡潔粹徹，得易本旨。〕

大傳論九卦之德之妙，以明處憂患之道也。夫易卦之德，周天下之用也。即九卦而德皆不偏焉，其於處憂患也何有？昔吾夫子大傳論九卦之德而再陳之，若謂易非聖人不能作，德非諸卦不能備。然或涉於一偏，未免滯於日用。是故禮者，順人情而非强世，若和矣；然品節詳明，事理精當，而實爲至焉。謙者，德欲盛而禮欲恭，若卑矣；然天道所益，人道所好，而尊且光焉。復以一陽生於羣陰之下，何其小也！然善端既復，欲不能間矣，豈以小而無辨乎？恒以一身混於紛華之中，何其雜也！然常德在我，久而不變矣，豈以雜而有厭乎？至若懲忿窒慾以脩身，損先焉難；從事既久，則無忿可懲，無慾可窒也，何易如之！遷善改過以長善，益實自裕；究而言之，則善所本有，過所本無也，何設之有？窮與通異，困爲柔揜，不能以自振者；但實德既脩，心無怨尤，無入而不自得矣。靜與動反，井居其所，不能以自
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: 〔Concise, refined, and penetrating; it grasps the fundamental purport of the Book of Changes.〕

The Great Commentary discusses the subtle excellence of the virtues of the nine hexagrams to illuminate the way to face anxiety and adversity. The virtues of the hexagrams of the Book of Changes encompass all applications under Heaven. Even within these nine hexagrams, the virtues are free of one-sidedness. What difficulty, then, could there be in facing anxiety and adversity? Formerly, our Master discussed the virtues of the nine hexagrams in the Great Commentary and set them forth a second time. It is as though he were saying that only a sage could compose the Changes, and that only through the various hexagrams could virtue be fully represented. Yet any lapse into one-sidedness would inevitably impede their application in daily life.

Thus ritual propriety [禮, apparently referring to the hexagram Treading, 履; ?] accords with human feelings without coercing the world, and so seems harmonious. Yet its distinctions and regulations are detailed and clear, and its handling of affairs and principles is precise and fitting: it truly reaches the utmost. In Modesty (Qian), virtue should be abundant and ritual conduct respectful, which seems lowly. Yet this is what the Way of Heaven augments and the way of humanity favors; hence it is honored and radiant. In Return (Fu), a single yang line arises beneath the many yin lines: how small it is! Yet once the beginnings of goodness have returned, desires cannot intrude. Could its smallness mean that it lacks discernment? In Constancy (Heng), one mingles personally amid the world's manifold splendors: how mixed it is! Yet enduring virtue resides within oneself and remains unchanged over time. Could such mingling bring weariness?

As for restraining anger and blocking desires in order to cultivate oneself, Decrease (Sun) is difficult at first. After sustained practice, however, there is no anger left to restrain and no desire left to block. What could be easier? Turning toward goodness and correcting faults to increase one's goodness, Increase (Yi) indeed brings enrichment from within. Ultimately, goodness is what one originally possesses, and faults are what one originally lacks. What need is there for contrivance?

Impediment differs from free passage. In Oppression (Kun), one is covered over by the yielding and cannot rouse oneself. Yet once genuine virtue has been cultivated, the heart harbors no resentment or blame, and one is at ease in every situation. Stillness is the opposite of movement. The Well (Jing) remains in its place and cannot, on its own, …

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
動者但剛中爲泉上出爲功自有利澤及物矣
以至巽德之制盖以一心之權度運萬用之機
宜經以處其常也權以通其變也泛應曲當又
何形迹之可窺乎噫君子反身脩德以處憂患
之道盖已盡於此矣抑考文王當羑里之時而
演易以憂患之情發之辭變象占之間皆開物
成務之意故夫子曰其辭危危者使平由是推
之六十四卦皆德也夫子獨陳九卦者偶舉此
以見例耳若乾言誠坤言敬敬立而誠存聖學
===
無餘事也又以見乾坤之理可以總括六十四
卦之蘊
書
肇十有二州封十有二山濬川
段有成
同考試官教諭戴批〔不蹈陳言自出一機軸簡潔明盡無慚此篇〕
考試官訓導穆批〔語意純正〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔分析明而有含蓄〕
punctuated:
動者，但剛中爲泉，上出爲功，自有利澤及物矣。以至巽德之制，盖以一心之權度，運萬用之機宜。經以處其常也，權以通其變也，泛應曲當，又何形迹之可窺乎？噫！君子反身脩德以處憂患之道，盖已盡於此矣。抑考文王當羑里之時而演易，以憂患之情發之，辭變象占之間，皆開物成務之意。故夫子曰：「其辭危，危者使平。」由是推之，六十四卦皆德也。夫子獨陳九卦者，偶舉此以見例耳。若乾言誠，坤言敬，敬立而誠存，聖學無餘事也。又以見乾坤之理，可以總括六十四卦之蘊。
書
肇十有二州，封十有二山，濬川。
段有成
同考試官教諭戴批〔不蹈陳言，自出一機軸，簡潔明盡，無慚此篇。〕
考試官訓導穆批〔語意純正。〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔分析明而有含蓄。〕
translation_en:
…move of itself; yet its firmness at the center constitutes the spring, and bringing water up constitutes its achievement. Thus its benefits naturally extend to other beings. As for the regulation exercised through the virtue of Xun (Compliance), this consists in using the weighing and measuring of a single mind to direct the appropriate responses to myriad circumstances. Constant principles address what is regular; discretionary judgment accommodates change. Responding to everything and fitting every particular, what outward traces could there be to discern? Ah! The gentleman’s way of turning inward to cultivate virtue and thereby meeting anxiety and adversity is surely fully set forth here.
Consider, moreover, how King Wen elaborated the Changes while at Youli, expressing his feelings of anxiety and adversity. Throughout its statements, transformations, images, and divinations runs the intention to disclose the nature of things and bring affairs to completion. Thus the Master said: “Its statements convey danger; awareness of danger brings peace.” By extension, all sixty-four hexagrams concern virtue. The Master singled out nine hexagrams simply as examples. Thus Qian speaks of sincerity, and Kun of reverence. When reverence is established and sincerity preserved, nothing further remains in the learning of the sages. This also shows that the principles of Qian and Kun can encompass the profound meanings of all sixty-four hexagrams.
Book of Documents
“He first established twelve provinces, designated twelve mountains, and dredged the rivers.”
Duan Youcheng
Comment by Associate Examiner Dai, Instructor: 〔He does not repeat stock expressions but devises an approach of his own. Concise, clear, and comprehensive: he need feel no shame for this composition.〕
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: 〔The language and meaning are pure and correct.〕
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: 〔The analysis is clear, while retaining implicit depth.〕

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
史臣記聖人疆理之周而防患之豫焉夫治莫
先於疆理而亦莫急於水患之防也聖人因舊
而增脩之亦惟其宜而已矣昔史臣之意若曰
人徒知有虞之治為無為而不知其初之大有
為也何則九州之制昉自中古及舜即位以冀
青之地視之他州為廣也於是始分冀之東為
并東北為幽又分青之東北為營也若夫九州
則惟仍其舊焉豈非所謂十二州乎增官屬溥
化理而吏治為之一新也九山之封其來已久
===
然州域既增則亦不可以無鎮也於是封營丘
於幽恒山於并又封醫無閭之山於營若夫九
山則惟因之而不改也豈非所謂十二山乎立
表識崇祝號而祀事為之有屬也九川滌源似
在不必濬矣舜則以為水患出於不測而備禦
在所當先乃為之脩利隄防以止其潰為之通
達溝瀆以開其障使凡十二州之水莫不各安
其所庶有以保平成之偉績也是則州之增非
侈也山之封非瀆也而川之濬又非過慮也皆
punctuated: 史臣記聖人疆理之周，而防患之豫焉。夫治莫先於疆理，而亦莫急於水患之防也。聖人因舊而增脩之，亦惟其宜而已矣。昔史臣之意若曰：人徒知有虞之治為無為，而不知其初之大有為也。何則？九州之制昉自中古，及舜即位，以冀青之地視之，他州為廣也。於是始分冀之東為并，東北為幽，又分青之東北為營也。若夫九州，則惟仍其舊焉。豈非所謂十二州乎？增官屬，溥化理，而吏治為之一新也。九山之封，其來已久，然州域既增，則亦不可以無鎮也。於是封營丘於幽，恒山於并，又封醫無閭之山於營。若夫九山，則惟因之而不改也。豈非所謂十二山乎？立表識，崇祝號，而祀事為之有屬也。九川滌源，似在不必濬矣。舜則以為水患出於不測，而備禦在所當先，乃為之脩利隄防以止其潰，為之通達溝瀆以開其障，使凡十二州之水莫不各安其所，庶有以保平成之偉績也。是則州之增非侈也，山之封非瀆也，而川之濬又非過慮也，皆
translation_en:
The court historian records the sage’s thoroughness in ordering territorial divisions and his foresight in preventing calamities. In government, nothing takes precedence over ordering territorial divisions, and nothing is more urgent than protection against floods. In adding to and improving the existing arrangements, the sage merely did what circumstances required. The ancient historian’s meaning might be expressed thus: people know only that the rule of Youyu was one of nonaction; they do not know how much purposeful action marked its beginnings. Why was this so? The system of nine provinces originated in middle antiquity. When Shun ascended the throne, the territories of Ji and Qing were found to be more extensive than those of the other provinces [?]. He therefore first divided off eastern Ji to form Bing, its northeastern portion to form You, and northeastern Qing to form Ying. As for the nine provinces, he retained their existing arrangements. Were these not the so-called twelve provinces? He increased the complement of officials and extended transforming instruction and good government, thereby renewing official administration.

The designation of the nine mountains had a long history. Yet, once the provincial territories had increased in number, they too could not lack their guardian mountains. He therefore designated Yingqiu in You [?], Mount Heng in Bing, and Mount Yiwulü in Ying. As for the nine mountains, he simply retained them without alteration. Were these not the so-called twelve mountains? He erected markers and exalted the titles used in ritual invocations, thereby assigning responsibility for sacrificial observances.

With the sources of the nine rivers cleared, further dredging might have seemed unnecessary. Shun, however, considered that floods arose unexpectedly and that defensive preparations must come first. He therefore repaired and improved the dikes and embankments to prevent breaches, and opened up the ditches and channels to remove obstructions. He ensured that the waters throughout the twelve provinces remained safely in their proper places, hoping thereby to preserve the great achievement of bringing the land and waters into order. Thus, increasing the number of provinces was no extravagance; designating the mountains was no impropriety in worship; and dredging the rivers was no excessive precaution. All were…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
行所無事而已聖人何心哉抑論之舜即位之
初汲汲焉惟土宇山川是務若於治不甚切者
殊不知體國經野乃先王之所以奉若天道舍
之不務其何以一道德而同風俗也哉噫帝舜
不復作矣然而萬世而下猶可以按迹職方興
思河洛謂非當時之功不可也
三八政一曰食二曰貨三曰祀四曰司空
五曰司徒六曰司寇七曰賓八曰師
陶賡
===
同考試官教諭戴批〔質而不俚秩而有序箕子演疇〕
〔之意藹然可見〕
考試官訓導穆批〔講八政處不晦不混宜錄以式〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔發揮得體〕
君子之演八政必以序而列其目也蓋王者之
政凡以為民但所係不能無緩急耳宜乎箕子
叙次之以告武王治天下之法也且其意若曰
禹因洛書左三之數而第為八政其理則因乎
天而不可易其用則切於民而不可離何以言
punctuated:
行所無事而已，聖人何心哉？抑論之，舜即位之初，汲汲焉惟土宇山川是務，若於治不甚切者。殊不知體國經野，乃先王之所以奉若天道，舍之不務，其何以一道德而同風俗也哉？噫！帝舜不復作矣。然而萬世而下，猶可以按迹職方，興思河洛，謂非當時之功不可也。
三、八政：一曰食，二曰貨，三曰祀，四曰司空，五曰司徒，六曰司寇，七曰賓，八曰師。
陶賡
同考試官教諭戴批〔質而不俚，秩而有序，箕子演疇〕〔之意藹然可見。〕
考試官訓導穆批〔講八政處，不晦不混，宜錄以式。〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔發揮得體。〕
君子之演八政，必以序而列其目也。蓋王者之政，凡以為民，但所係不能無緩急耳。宜乎箕子叙次之，以告武王治天下之法也。且其意若曰：禹因洛書左三之數，而第為八政，其理則因乎天而不可易，其用則切於民而不可離。何以言
translation_en:
…merely proceeding without forcing matters. What private purpose could the sage have had? Yet consider this: at the beginning of Shun’s reign, he urgently devoted himself to the territory, mountains, and rivers, seemingly matters of no immediate importance to government. This overlooks the fact that organizing the state and demarcating the countryside were the means by which the former kings reverently followed the Way of Heaven. If these tasks were abandoned, how could moral principles be unified and customs made alike? Alas! Emperor Shun will never arise again. Yet even ten thousand generations later, we can still examine the traces of his work in the records of regional administration and ponder the Yellow and Luo Rivers. We cannot deny that this is owing to his achievements at that time.
3. “The eight affairs of government: the first is food; the second, goods; the third, sacrifices; the fourth, the Minister of Works; the fifth, the Minister of Education; the sixth, the Minister of Justice; the seventh, guests; and the eighth, the army.”
Tao Geng
Comment by Associate Examiner Dai, Instructor: 〔Substantial without being vulgar, orderly and well arranged: Jizi’s intention in expounding the categories〕〔is abundantly apparent.〕
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: 〔The discussion of the eight affairs of government is neither obscure nor confused. It should be recorded as a model.〕
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: 〔The exposition is appropriate.〕
When a gentleman expounds the eight affairs of government, he must enumerate their headings in due order. All the measures of a true king’s government are for the people, but the matters they concern necessarily differ in urgency. It was therefore fitting that Jizi arranged them in sequence to instruct King Wu in the method of governing all under Heaven. His meaning was, moreover, as though he said: Yu followed the number three on the left of the Luo Writing and placed the eight affairs of government third. Their underlying principles follow Heaven and cannot be altered; their application closely concerns the people and cannot be dispensed with. How can this be explained…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
之彼民無食則無以為命而重農力本在所當
先故一曰食焉非貨則無以為資而阜財惠商
亦不容緩故二曰貨焉生養遂而孝敬生則祭
以報本亦理之所不容已者是以有祀焉而列
之於三然民不可渙散而無居則有司空掌土
而宮室之制興故居四焉亦不可逸居而無教
則有司徒掌教而學校之建廣故居五焉道化
尼而淫慝作則刑以禁姦亦勢之所不能免者
是以有司寇之設而序之於六人情非禮不通
===
於是乎有賓以親邦國賓處乎順故居七焉禍
亂非兵不弭於是乎有師以平邦國師權乎變
是以居末而為八政之終事焉為治者果能行
此則民生無不厚而彝倫又豈有不叙者哉抑
因是而考之武王焉重民五教惟食喪祭而六
典建官終周世不改孰謂非箕子啓之耶至於
所以為之則又本之人君之心是以列五事於
八政之先而首以敬用為言故曰必有關睢麟
趾之意然後可以行周官之法度
punctuated: 之？彼民無食，則無以為命，而重農力本在所當先，故一曰食焉。非貨，則無以為資，而阜財惠商亦不容緩，故二曰貨焉。生養遂而孝敬生，則祭以報本，亦理之所不容已者，是以有祀焉，而列之於三。然民不可渙散而無居，則有司空掌土，而宮室之制興，故居四焉。亦不可逸居而無教，則有司徒掌教，而學校之建廣，故居五焉。道化尼而淫慝作，則刑以禁姦，亦勢之所不能免者，是以有司寇之設，而序之於六。人情非禮不通，於是乎有賓以親邦國。賓處乎順，故居七焉。禍亂非兵不弭，於是乎有師以平邦國。師權乎變，是以居末，而為八政之終事焉。為治者果能行此，則民生無不厚，而彝倫又豈有不叙者哉？抑因是而考之武王焉，重民五教，惟食喪祭，而六典建官，終周世不改，孰謂非箕子啓之耶？至於所以為之，則又本之人君之心，是以列五事於八政之先，而首以敬用為言。故曰：「必有關睢麟趾之意，然後可以行周官之法度。」
translation_en:
… explain this? Without food, the people have no means of sustaining life. Giving priority to agriculture and exerting effort in this fundamental occupation must therefore come first; hence the first item is food. Without goods, they have no resources to draw upon. Increasing wealth and benefiting merchants likewise admit of no delay; hence the second item is goods. When their livelihood and nurture are secured, filial devotion and reverence arise. Offering sacrifices to repay their origins is then something that principle does not permit them to neglect. Thus there are sacrifices, ranked third. Yet the people cannot be left scattered and without dwellings. There is therefore a Minister of Works to administer the land, and arrangements for buildings and dwellings are established; hence this office ranks fourth. Nor may the people live at ease without instruction. There is therefore a Minister of Education to oversee instruction, and schools are widely established; hence this office ranks fifth. When moral instruction is obstructed and depravity arises, using punishments to restrain wrongdoing is also something circumstances make unavoidable. Thus the office of Minister of Justice is established and ranked sixth. Human sentiments cannot be communicated without ritual propriety; hence there is the reception of guests, to foster amity among the states. Receiving guests belongs to the orderly course of affairs, and therefore ranks seventh. Calamity and disorder cannot be quelled without armed force; hence there is the army, to pacify the states. Military action requires discretionary responses to changing circumstances, so it is placed last, as the final undertaking among the eight measures of government. If those who govern can truly carry these out, the people's livelihood will be amply provided for in every respect. How, then, could the enduring human relationships fail to be properly ordered?

Let us further examine King Wu in light of this. He attached importance to the people and the five teachings, and attended to food, mourning, and sacrifice. Officials were established under the six canons of government, and this arrangement remained unchanged throughout the Zhou dynasty. Who could say that it was not Jizi who enlightened him? As for the means of putting these things into practice, their root lies in the ruler's own heart. Thus the five personal affairs are placed before the eight measures of government, introduced with the injunction to apply them reverently. Hence the saying: “Only when one possesses the spirit of ‘The Ospreys Cry’ (Guanju) and ‘The Qilin's Hoofs’ (Linzhi) can one put into practice the laws and institutions of the Offices of Zhou.”

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
詩
王命召伯定申伯之宅登是南邦世執其
功
楊茂時
同考試官訓導許批〔推本黍苗以著城謝之功於世執處以作式為輔為說自非他作可及〕
考試官訓導穆批〔先王封申伯之意是如此〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔溫潤詳盡錄之〕
周王封親臣有以建其業而欲以永其傳也夫
===
建國而命大臣親之可謂致重矣使傳之不永
又何以裕其後哉宣王之舅申伯出封于謝尹
吉甫作詩以送之及此若謂申伯之生也嶽實
降神而其功也懋在王室謝邑之封何如哉彼
立國建侯周之懿典也王以召伯而授厥命使
之因是謝人以經營其居列爵分土國有常經
也召伯以司空而任若事于焉率彼烝徒以大
啟其宇以定經制以辨章程奠雄鎮于一方肅
爾謝功于是乎告成矣原隰水泉之治墉垣家
punctuated:
詩

「王命召伯，定申伯之宅，登是南邦，世執其功。」

楊茂時

同考試官訓導許批〔推本黍苗以著城謝之功，於世執處以作式為輔為說，自非他作可及。〕

考試官訓導穆批〔先王封申伯之意是如此。〕

考試官教諭鄭批〔溫潤詳盡，錄之。〕

周王封親臣，有以建其業而欲以永其傳也。夫建國而命大臣親之，可謂致重矣。使傳之不永，又何以裕其後哉？宣王之舅申伯出封于謝，尹吉甫作詩以送之。及此，若謂申伯之生也，嶽實降神；而其功也，懋在王室。謝邑之封何如哉？彼立國建侯，周之懿典也。王以召伯而授厥命，使之因是謝人以經營其居。列爵分土，國有常經也。召伯以司空而任若事，于焉率彼烝徒，以大啟其宇，以定經制，以辨章程。奠雄鎮于一方，肅爾謝功，于是乎告成矣。原隰水泉之治，墉垣家
translation_en:
Book of Odes

“The king commanded the Earl of Shao to establish the Earl of Shen’s residence, to raise up this southern state, and to have its achievements maintained through the generations.”

Yang Maoshi

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Assistant Instructor: 〔By tracing the matter back to “Millet Seedlings,” the essay brings out the achievement of fortifying Xie. In explaining “maintained through the generations,” it develops the ideas of serving as a model and acting as a support. Other compositions certainly cannot match it.〕

Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: 〔Such was the former king’s intention in enfeoffing the Earl of Shen.〕

Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: 〔Gentle and polished, thorough and complete. Include it in the record.〕

When the king of Zhou enfeoffed a minister who was his kinsman, he provided the means to establish that minister’s undertaking and wished to perpetuate its transmission. To establish a state and command a great minister to attend personally to it may indeed be called treating the matter with the utmost weight. But if its transmission were not enduring, how could provision be made for his descendants?

King Xuan’s maternal uncle, the Earl of Shen, went out to receive his fief at Xie, and Yin Jifu composed an ode to send him off. At this point, the ode seems to say: at the Earl of Shen’s birth, the sacred mountain truly sent down its spiritual power, and his meritorious service to the royal house was outstanding. What, then, was involved in his enfeoffment at Xie?

Establishing states and investing lords was an admirable institution of Zhou. The king entrusted his command to the Earl of Shao, directing him to draw upon the people of Xie to lay out and build the Earl of Shen’s residence. Apportioning ranks and dividing lands were enduring principles of the state. The Earl of Shao, as Minister of Works, took responsibility for this undertaking. Thereupon he led the assembled workers to enlarge its precincts, establish its institutional arrangements, and distinguish its regulations. A mighty stronghold was established in that region; the solemn undertaking at Xie was thus announced complete. The ordering of the uplands and lowlands, the waterways and springs, the walls and homes…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
室之立慰王心于九重翼翼南國于是乎底績
矣然此豈特示寵異于一時大封拜于今日而
已哉蓋繼序其皇君之所以望臣也將俾世其
職者保有成業于以衍國祚於靈長不顯亦世
士之所以生周也將俾作之後者念茲戎功于
以綿國脉于悠乆世德之作求永為南國之式
後之繼申猶申之繼甫也而藩翰者有所藉矣
舊服之纘承恒為周室之輔後賢之繼述有光
于上世之開承也而于宣者有所賴矣是則申
===
===
伯之封非倖致宣王之錫非濫及有周封建之
典于是可見而吉甫播揚以為贈也固宜抑論
申伯以元舅之親出封于謝宣王豈直為親親
已也蓋申伯德業聞望足為當時之重而謝之
為邑實作鎮于南土所以鎮定而綏服之者亦
不可匪其人也崧高之作反覆於藩翰作式為
憲之說而激勸感發之意默寓其間故讀其詩
則宣王親賢懷遠之道當時友朋勸示之益俱
可想見于千載之上
punctuated:
室之立，慰王心于九重，翼翼南國，于是乎底績矣。然此豈特示寵異于一時，大封拜于今日而已哉？蓋「繼序其皇」，君之所以望臣也。將俾世其職者保有成業，于以衍國祚於靈長。「不顯亦世」，士之所以生周也。將俾作之後者念茲戎功，于以綿國脉于悠乆。世德之作求，永為南國之式，後之繼申，猶申之繼甫也，而藩翰者有所藉矣。舊服之纘承，恒為周室之輔，後賢之繼述，有光于上世之開承也，而于宣者有所賴矣。是則申伯之封非倖致，宣王之錫非濫及，有周封建之典于是可見，而吉甫播揚以為贈也固宜。
抑論申伯以元舅之親出封于謝，宣王豈直為親親已也？蓋申伯德業聞望足為當時之重，而謝之為邑實作鎮于南土，所以鎮定而綏服之者，亦不可匪其人也。《崧高》之作，反覆於藩翰、作式、為憲之說，而激勸感發之意默寓其間。故讀其詩，則宣王親賢懷遠之道、當時友朋勸示之益，俱可想見于千載之上。
translation_en:
…and the construction of dwellings comforted the king’s heart deep within his palace. The orderly southern states thus saw the work brought to completion. Yet was this merely to display exceptional favor for a moment and bestow a great enfeoffment today? Surely, “continuing the succession and magnifying it” expresses what a ruler expects of his ministers. He would have those who inherit their offices preserve their established achievements, thereby extending the state’s good fortune far into the future. “Illustrious through successive generations” expresses how worthy men sustain Zhou [?]. He would have those who arise as successors remember these great achievements, thereby perpetuating the state’s vitality for ages to come. By seeking to carry forward ancestral virtue, they would forever serve as models for the southern states. Those who later succeed Shen would be like Shen succeeding Fu, and the realm would have men on whom to depend as its protective bulwarks. By inheriting their longstanding duties, they would always serve as supports of the house of Zhou. The continuation of this work by worthy successors would bring glory to what earlier generations had founded and transmitted [?], and King Xuan would have men on whom to rely [?]. Thus Shen Bo’s enfeoffment was no stroke of undeserved fortune, nor was King Xuan’s grant indiscriminately bestowed. Here one can see the Zhou institutions for establishing fiefs and conferring lordships. It was certainly fitting that Jifu should celebrate this in a poem presented as a parting gift.
Moreover, consider Shen Bo’s departure to receive his fief at Xie, as the king’s senior maternal uncle. Could King Xuan have been acting solely out of affection for his kin? Shen Bo’s virtue, accomplishments, reputation, and standing were sufficient to make him a leading figure of his age, while Xie itself served as a stronghold in the southern lands. The man charged with securing those lands, pacifying them, and bringing them into allegiance therefore had to be suited to the task. The poem “Lofty Mountains” (Song gao) repeatedly speaks of serving as a bulwark, setting an example, and providing a standard, quietly embedding within these expressions the intention to exhort, encourage, move, and inspire. Thus, in reading this poem, one can envision, across more than a thousand years, both King Xuan’s way of drawing worthy men close and winning over distant peoples, and the benefits of the exhortation and guidance exchanged among friends in that age.

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
於皇武王無競維烈允文文王克開厥後
嗣武受之勝殷遏劉耆定爾功
楊錫文
同考試官訓導許批模寫周公象功作樂之意明白
可錄
考試官訓導穆批講題意能知輕重取之
考試官教諭鄭批腴而整
詩人頌王者有大功必表其因所啓以成功也
蓋周有天下固武王之功而啓之者則文王也
===
詩人推本而言之也有以夫此周公象武王之
功爲大武之樂首之以嗟嘆之詞若曰大哉武
王之爲君也聖武布昭而興王之績上格于天
皇靈丕振而創造之功有隆于古其烈之盛天
下無得而競矣然豈無所自哉蓋允矣思文之
文王也脩和有夏而維新之命有以立後世仰
承之基開國之規模固自岐周而肇啓矣輯寧
邦家而有二之業足以爲後人憑藉之地興周
之氣象固自遷豐而光顯矣故我武王之嗣興
punctuated:
於皇武王，無競維烈！允文文王，克開厥後。嗣武受之，勝殷遏劉，耆定爾功。
楊錫文
同考試官訓導許批：模寫周公象功作樂之意，明白可錄。
考試官訓導穆批：講題意，能知輕重，取之。
考試官教諭鄭批：腴而整。
詩人頌王者有大功，必表其因所啓以成功也。蓋周有天下，固武王之功，而啓之者則文王也。詩人推本而言之也，有以夫！此周公象武王之功爲大武之樂，首之以嗟嘆之詞，若曰：大哉，武王之爲君也！聖武布昭，而興王之績上格于天；皇靈丕振，而創造之功有隆于古。其烈之盛，天下無得而競矣。然豈無所自哉？蓋允矣，思文之文王也！脩和有夏，而維新之命有以立後世仰承之基，開國之規模固自岐周而肇啓矣；輯寧邦家，而有二之業足以爲後人憑藉之地，興周之氣象固自遷豐而光顯矣。故我武王之嗣興
translation_en:
“Ah, august King Wu! Unrivaled were his achievements! Truly cultured was King Wen, who opened the way for his successors. Succeeding him, Wu received his legacy, conquered Yin, checked slaughter, and firmly established your achievement.”
Yang Xiwen
Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Assistant Instructor: “His depiction of the Duke of Zhou’s intention in making music to represent the achievements is clear and merits inclusion.”
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: “In expounding the meaning of the topic, he understands the relative weight of its parts. Accept it.”
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “Rich and well ordered.”
When the poet praises a king’s great achievements, he invariably makes clear the prior groundwork upon which their accomplishment depended. For although Zhou’s possession of all under Heaven was indeed King Wu’s achievement, it was King Wen who opened the way. The poet had good reason to trace it to its source!
Here the Duke of Zhou composed the music of the Great Martial Dance (Dawu) to represent King Wu’s achievements, beginning with words of admiration, as though saying: Great indeed was King Wu as a ruler! His sagely martial might shone far and wide, and his accomplishment in establishing the royal house reached Heaven above. His august spiritual power was mightily displayed, and his achievement in founding the dynasty surpassed those of antiquity. Such was the greatness of his deeds that none under Heaven could rival them. Yet could they have been without a source?
Truly, it was the cultured King Wen! He cultivated harmony throughout the Xia lands, and the renewed Mandate thereby laid a foundation that later generations could reverently inherit. The design for founding the state thus had its beginnings in Qizhou. He brought peace to the realm, and his achievement in possessing two-thirds of it provided ground upon which his successors could rely. The promise of Zhou’s rise thus became manifest with the move to Feng. Therefore, when our King Wu arose as his successor …

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
也思寵受之重而致駿惠之功於鑠之師旣興
戎衣一著遂勝殷于牧野純熈之時旣會大介
是用因止殺于崇朝由是上而天命于周而有
僕允陟元后而一代之大業以成維揚之武視
文考而有光也下而人心于周而攸同奄有萬
方而帝王之大統以集丕承之烈蓋自今而致
定也夫功雖開于文王而實成于武王此武王
之功所以爲大也歟抑是詩也雖象武功而作
孔子之論樂極于周道四達禮樂交通有聲之
===
雅亦曰皇王維辟無思不服武王之有天下固
非以力取之者而允文文王有此武功亦非不
足于武可知矣前後相承文武並用所以創成
周八百年之業非偶然也大武桓賚之歌揚之
宗廟三復之猶可想見其盛
春秋
遂伐楚僖公四年諸侯遂救許僖公六年
黨璽
考試官訓導穆批善發褒貶齊桓之意
punctuated:
也，思寵受之重而致駿惠之功。於鑠之師旣興，戎衣一著，遂勝殷于牧野；純熈之時旣會，大介是用，因止殺于崇朝。由是，上而天命于周而有僕，允陟元后，而一代之大業以成，維揚之武視文考而有光也；下而人心于周而攸同，奄有萬方，而帝王之大統以集，丕承之烈蓋自今而致定也。夫功雖開于文王，而實成于武王，此武王之功所以爲大也歟！抑是詩也，雖象武功而作，孔子之論樂極于周道四達、禮樂交通，《有聲》之雅亦曰：「皇王維辟，無思不服。」武王之有天下，固非以力取之者，而允文文王有此武功，亦非不足于武可知矣。前後相承，文武並用，所以創成周八百年之業，非偶然也。《大武》《桓》《賚》之歌揚之宗廟，三復之，猶可想見其盛。

春秋
「遂伐楚」，僖公四年；「諸侯遂救許」，僖公六年。
黨璽
考試官訓導穆批：「善發褒貶齊桓之意。」
translation_en:
…when King Wu succeeded to the throne, he reflected upon the weight of the favor he had received and accomplished the great work of following his predecessor’s example. Once his glorious army had arisen, he donned his battle dress and defeated Yin at Muye. When the moment of pure brilliance arrived, he put on his great armor [?] and brought the killing to an end within a single morning. Thus, above, Heaven’s mandate attached itself to Zhou: he truly ascended as sovereign, and the great undertaking of a dynasty was accomplished. His martial prowess, magnificently displayed, added luster to that of his deceased father, King Wen. Below, the hearts of the people united in allegiance to Zhou: he possessed the myriad regions, and the great imperial succession devolved upon him. His glorious achievement in carrying forward his inheritance was henceforth firmly established. Although King Wen began the undertaking, King Wu actually completed it. Is this not why King Wu’s achievement was so great?

Yet although this ode was composed to represent martial achievement, Confucius’s discussion of its music culminated in the Way of Zhou reaching in all four directions and ritual and music circulating everywhere. The Greater Court Hymn “There Is a Sound” (You sheng) likewise says: “The august king is sovereign; none thinks of withholding submission.” King Wu’s possession of All-under-Heaven was certainly not something he secured through force alone. And we may also recognize that King Wen, truly accomplished in civil virtue, possessed these martial achievements and was by no means deficient in military prowess. Predecessor and successor carried on the same work, employing both civil and martial capacities. Their founding and completion of Zhou’s eight-hundred-year enterprise was no accident. The songs of the Great Martial Dance (Da wu), “Martial Prowess” (Huan), and “Bestowal” (Lai) proclaimed this in the ancestral temple. Chanting them repeatedly, one can still envision its splendor.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“They thereupon attacked Chu”—fourth year of Duke Xi. “The feudal lords thereupon relieved Xu”—sixth year of Duke Xi.

Dang Xi

Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor, comments: “Skillfully brings out the intent behind the praise and censure of Duke Huan of Qi.”

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
考試官教諭鄭批嚴整可錄
伯主攘外失於專春秋譏之恤小合於義春秋
善之此楚之伐許之救而齊覇之得失判矣且
伐楚者齊桓公也伐之何如曰爲其久病中國
也久病中國而伐之功弗少矣君子顧於桓乎
譏之何曰爲其失於專征也征伐自天子出受
命于祖受成于學非臣下可得而擅也桓公是
舉不待天王之命爰興八國之師彤弓未錫而
閫制自由牙璋未啓而天討奚在意文武之建
===
侯也以蕃王室也賢如桓吾方望其宗周而先
天下也今也討有罪之國而已涉無王之嫌主
中夏之盟而首犯先王之令回視羲和之征桓
不逮胤侯遠矣書曰臣無作威桓其昧之經書
伐而曰遂者譏其專也此義行則蔑視君父者
懼而君臣之分嚴矣哉救許者亦齊桓公也救
之何如曰爲其近罹楚禍也近罹楚禍而救之
事亦常耳君子顧於桓乎善之何曰爲其急於
救患也夷虜爲中國患如火斯焚如水斯溺非
punctuated:
考試官教諭鄭批：嚴整可錄。

伯主攘外，失於專，春秋譏之；恤小，合於義，春秋善之。此楚之伐、許之救，而齊覇之得失判矣。且伐楚者，齊桓公也。伐之何如？曰：爲其久病中國也。久病中國而伐之，功弗少矣。君子顧於桓乎譏之，何？曰：爲其失於專征也。征伐自天子出，受命于祖，受成于學，非臣下可得而擅也。桓公是舉，不待天王之命，爰興八國之師。彤弓未錫，而閫制自由；牙璋未啓，而天討奚在？意文武之建侯也，以蕃王室也。賢如桓，吾方望其宗周而先天下也。今也，討有罪之國，而已涉無王之嫌；主中夏之盟，而首犯先王之令。回視羲和之征，桓不逮胤侯遠矣。《書》曰：「臣無作威。」桓其昧之。經書伐而曰遂者，譏其專也。此義行，則蔑視君父者懼，而君臣之分嚴矣哉！救許者，亦齊桓公也。救之何如？曰：爲其近罹楚禍也。近罹楚禍而救之，事亦常耳。君子顧於桓乎善之，何？曰：爲其急於救患也。夷虜爲中國患，如火斯焚，如水斯溺，非
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zheng, an Instructor: “Rigorous and well ordered; worthy of inclusion.”

When the hegemon repelled outsiders but erred in acting on his sole authority, the Spring and Autumn Annals censured him; when he aided a small state in accordance with righteousness, the Spring and Autumn Annals commended him. Thus, in the attack on Chu and the relief of Xu, the merits and faults of Qi’s hegemony are clearly distinguished. Now, the man who attacked Chu was Duke Huan of Qi. How should his attack be judged? The answer is: Chu had long afflicted the Central States. To attack a state that had long afflicted the Central States was no small achievement. Why, then, does the gentleman nevertheless censure Duke Huan? The answer is: he erred in undertaking a punitive expedition on his sole authority. Punitive expeditions proceed from the Son of Heaven: the commander receives his mandate in the ancestral temple and the settled plan at the school. These are not matters that a subject may presume to undertake on his own. In this action, Duke Huan did not await the Heavenly King’s command before raising the armies of eight states. Before a red bow had been bestowed upon him, he exercised military command at his own discretion; before the toothed jade tablet had been issued to authorize mobilization, what warrant was there for punishment in Heaven’s name? Consider how Kings Wen and Wu established the feudal lords: it was to protect the royal house. From one as worthy as Duke Huan, I would have expected reverence for Zhou and leadership of all under Heaven in that reverence. Yet now, in punishing a guilty state, he had already incurred suspicion of disregarding the king; in presiding over the covenants of the Central States, he was the first to violate the former kings’ commands. Looking back to the expedition against Xi and He, Duke Huan fell far short of the Marquis of Yin. The Book of Documents says: “Let no subject exercise sovereign coercive power.” Duke Huan seems to have been ignorant of this. When the Classic records the attack with the word “thereupon,” it censures his unilateral action. If this principle prevails, those who disdain their ruler or father will be afraid, and the distinction between ruler and subject will indeed be strictly maintained!

The man who relieved Xu was also Duke Huan of Qi. How should his relief of Xu be judged? The answer is: Xu had recently suffered calamity at Chu’s hands. To relieve a state that had recently suffered calamity at Chu’s hands was merely an ordinary undertaking. Why, then, does the gentleman nevertheless commend Duke Huan? The answer is: he acted urgently to relieve distress. When barbarians afflict the Central States, it is like being burned by fire or drowned by water; it is not…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
盟主所得緩焉者也桓之是役不待逾時之久
卽移六國之兵楚旅還轅而外侮以禦許人安
堵而小國以寧噫湯文之字小也以除暴橫也
强如桓吾方恐其討鄭而忽許難也今也遏荐
食之謀而凶暴有所懲解倒懸之厄而弱小有
所恃回視凡伯之伐桓其過衞宣遠矣詩曰戎
狄是膺桓其以之經書救而曰遂者善之尤也
此義行則輕棄諸姬者懼而恤患之義昭矣哉
是則伐而書遂貶其遂也救而書遂褒其遂也
===
所謂美惡不嫌同辭其此之謂夫抑伐楚過矣
難掩夫服楚之功救許功矣難掩夫失黃之過
此伯者假之之私而非若王者之純乎公也然
考之當時王政不行諸侯僭亂而為桓公者猶
知以尊周攘夷為念兵車之屬六乘車之會三
帥諸侯而朝天子使天下猶知有共主焉則其
有功於周室亦不淺矣桓其可盡訾哉
晉人執鄭伯欒書帥師伐鄭成公九年
楊本聰
punctuated:
盟主所得緩焉者也。桓之是役，不待逾時之久，卽移六國之兵。楚旅還轅，而外侮以禦；許人安堵，而小國以寧。噫！湯文之字小也，以除暴橫也。强如桓，吾方恐其討鄭而忽許難也。今也遏荐食之謀，而凶暴有所懲；解倒懸之厄，而弱小有所恃。回視凡伯之伐，桓其過衞宣遠矣。《詩》曰：「戎狄是膺。」桓其以之。經書救而曰遂者，善之尤也。此義行，則輕棄諸姬者懼，而恤患之義昭矣哉！是則伐而書遂，貶其遂也；救而書遂，褒其遂也。所謂美惡不嫌同辭，其此之謂夫！抑伐楚過矣，難掩夫服楚之功；救許功矣，難掩夫失黃之過。此伯者假之之私，而非若王者之純乎公也。然考之當時，王政不行，諸侯僭亂，而為桓公者，猶知以尊周攘夷為念。兵車之屬六，乘車之會三，帥諸侯而朝天子，使天下猶知有共主焉，則其有功於周室亦不淺矣。桓其可盡訾哉？

晉人執鄭伯，欒書帥師伐鄭。成公九年。
楊本聰。
translation_en:
…a matter in which the leader of the alliance could afford to delay. In this campaign, Duke Huan promptly redirected the armies of six states, without waiting for any considerable time to elapse. The troops of Chu turned their chariots homeward, and foreign aggression was repelled; the people of Xu remained secure in their homes, and the small state enjoyed peace. Ah! When Tang and King Wen cherished small states, their purpose was to eliminate violence and oppression. With someone as powerful as Duke Huan, I had feared that he would punish Zheng while neglecting Xu’s distress. Yet now he checked the plan to devour states one after another, thereby chastening the violent; he relieved a predicament like being suspended upside down, giving the weak and small someone on whom to rely. Looking back at the attack on Fan Bo, Duke Huan far surpassed Duke Xuan of Wei. The Book of Odes says, “Strike against the Rong and Di.” Duke Huan acted accordingly. When the Classic records the rescue and uses the word “thereupon,” it expresses particular approval. If this principle prevails, those who lightly abandon the states of the Ji lineage will be afraid, and the duty to relieve distress will be manifest! Thus, when an attack is recorded with “thereupon,” his proceeding on his own initiative is condemned; when a rescue is recorded with “thereupon,” his proceeding on his own initiative is praised. Surely this is what is meant by saying that praise and blame need not avoid using the same wording!

Yet although attacking Chu was a fault, it cannot obscure his achievement in bringing Chu to submission; although rescuing Xu was an achievement, it cannot obscure his fault in allowing Huang to be lost. Such is the self-interest of a hegemon who borrows the practice of virtue, unlike a true king whose actions are wholly devoted to the common good. Nevertheless, if we examine the circumstances of the time, royal government was no longer effective, and the regional lords were usurping authority and creating disorder. Even so, Duke Huan still knew to concern himself with honoring Zhou and repelling the barbarians. He assembled the lords with war chariots six times and held meetings with ceremonial carriages three times. He led the regional lords in paying court to the Son of Heaven, ensuring that all under Heaven still recognized a common sovereign. His service to the royal house of Zhou was therefore considerable. Can Duke Huan be condemned without qualification?

“The men of Jin seized the Earl of Zheng; Luan Shu led an army to attack Zheng.” Ninth year of Duke Cheng.

Yang Bencong.

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
考試官訓導穆批〔辭不煩而有斷制深得謹嚴之旨〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔不失傳意〕
春秋紀伯討之非有所以明大分者有所以正
大防者此見春秋之義不可以一端求也且鄭
懷楚賂而會楚晉惡鄭貳而討鄭乃因鄭成之
朝而執於銅鞮隨遣欒書伐其國焉夫晉本侯
也窮諸人何居邦典定諸侯之獄司隸掌執人
之事大司寇之職周官之法度不可干也鄭固
===
罪矣晉始執也不以王命既執也不歸京師君
子曰執而無命則不臣不臣則不爵窮諸人賤
之也豈復得為伯討乎於時伯蠲行成晉戮之
矣略而不紀者何曰天下有大分君臣是已成
非蠲之君蠲非成之臣耶君實有國神之主而
民之望也成執于晉進退惟其所制榮辱莫之
或知國之患莫大乎此蠲之身庸足多乎傳曰
既執其君矣則行人為輕明此則天下皆知君
之為重而後其君者寡矣貴有常尊大分不既
punctuated:
考試官訓導穆批〔辭不煩而有斷制，深得謹嚴之旨〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔不失傳意〕
春秋紀伯討之非，有所以明大分者，有所以正大防者。此見春秋之義，不可以一端求也。且鄭懷楚賂而會楚，晉惡鄭貳而討鄭，乃因鄭成之朝而執於銅鞮，隨遣欒書伐其國焉。夫晉本侯也，窮諸人何居？邦典定諸侯之獄，司隸掌執人之事，大司寇之職，周官之法度不可干也。鄭固罪矣，晉始執也，不以王命；既執也，不歸京師。君子曰：「執而無命，則不臣；不臣，則不爵。」窮諸人，賤之也，豈復得為伯討乎？於時伯蠲行成，晉戮之矣。略而不紀者何？曰：天下有大分，君臣是已。成非蠲之君，蠲非成之臣耶？君實有國，神之主而民之望也。成執于晉，進退惟其所制，榮辱莫之或知，國之患莫大乎此。蠲之身，庸足多乎？傳曰：「既執其君矣，則行人為輕。」明此，則天下皆知君之為重，而後其君者寡矣。貴有常尊，大分不既
translation_en:
Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The wording is economical yet decisive, thoroughly capturing the intent of scrupulous precision.〕
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: 〔It preserves the meaning of the commentary.〕
In recording the wrongfulness of punitive expeditions undertaken by hegemons, the Spring and Autumn Annals sometimes elucidates the fundamental distinctions of status and sometimes rectifies the fundamental boundaries. This shows that the meaning of the Annals cannot be sought from a single perspective. Zheng, cherishing Chu’s gifts, met with Chu; Jin, resenting Zheng’s divided allegiance, punished Zheng. Taking advantage of Duke Cheng of Zheng’s court visit, Jin detained him at Tongdi and then dispatched Luan Shu to attack his state. Now the ruler of Jin was himself a lord: why was he reduced to the designation “men”? Under the statutes of the realm, adjudicating cases involving the regional lords, and the Director of Convict Labor’s responsibility for taking people into custody, belonged to the jurisdiction of the Minister of Justice [?]. The institutions of the Offices of Zhou could not be infringed. Zheng was certainly guilty, but when Jin first detained its ruler, it did so without the king’s command; after detaining him, it did not deliver him to the royal capital. The gentleman says: “To detain someone without a command is to fail in one’s duty as a subject; one who fails in that duty is not accorded his noble title.” Reducing Jin to the designation “men” debases it. How could this still qualify as a hegemon’s punitive expedition?
At that time, Bo Juan went to negotiate peace, and Jin executed him. Why is this omitted rather than recorded? The answer is: the world has a fundamental distinction of status—that between ruler and subject. Was Cheng not Juan’s ruler, and Juan not Cheng’s subject? The ruler possesses the state, presides over its spirits, and is the focus of the people’s hopes. Cheng was detained in Jin; his movements were entirely subject to its control, and no one knew whether honor or humiliation awaited him. No calamity for a state could be greater than this. How could Juan’s own person merit much weight? The commentary says: “Once they had detained his ruler, the envoy was of lesser consequence.” Once this is understood, all under Heaven will recognize the ruler’s importance, and few will put their ruler second. Those of exalted rank have an enduring claim to honor; has not the fundamental distinction of status already …

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
定矣哉於時楚子重侵陳以救鄭矣削而不書
者何曰天下有大防夷夏是巳晉非禮義之國
楚非禽獸與隣者耶景雖不競猶主夏盟者也
鄭附于楚德之不懷而威焉是畏親之不篤而
利焉是從變之不善一至於此楚之救庸足多
乎傳曰鄭無可救之善楚不得有能救之名明
此則天下皆知夷之可鄙而變於夷者鮮矣夷
不亂華大防不既嚴矣哉于以見聖人之筆削
無非為君臣夷夏計也國史焉得而與夫抑楚
===
奚待責乎鄭奚足責乎晉景嗣伯中國所仰無
亦以德禮招携懷遠乎鄭與楚合而即來朝過
而悔矣執其身伐其國戮其使暴也夫召陵之
禮楚使蕭魚信鄭不疑桓乎悼乎賢於景也遠
矣雖然仲知有以教之也景不桓不悼也臣又
不仲不知也禮信焉攸施故曰為政在人
禮記
故聖人參於天地並於鬼神以治政也
梁佐
punctuated:
定矣哉？於時楚子重侵陳以救鄭矣，削而不書者何？曰：天下有大防，夷夏是巳。晉非禮義之國，楚非禽獸與隣者耶？景雖不競，猶主夏盟者也。鄭附于楚，德之不懷而威焉是畏，親之不篤而利焉是從，變之不善一至於此，楚之救庸足多乎？傳曰：「鄭無可救之善，楚不得有能救之名。」明此，則天下皆知夷之可鄙，而變於夷者鮮矣。夷不亂華，大防不既嚴矣哉？于以見聖人之筆削，無非為君臣夷夏計也，國史焉得而與？夫抑楚奚待責乎？鄭奚足責乎？晉景嗣伯，中國所仰，無亦以德禮招携懷遠乎？鄭與楚合而即來朝，過而悔矣。執其身，伐其國，戮其使，暴也夫！召陵之禮楚使，蕭魚信鄭不疑，桓乎！悼乎！賢於景也遠矣。雖然，仲知有以教之也。景不桓不悼也，臣又不仲不知也，禮信焉攸施？故曰：「為政在人。」

《禮記》
故聖人參於天地，並於鬼神，以治政也。
梁佐
translation_en:
…firmly established? At that time, Zizhong of Chu invaded Chen to rescue Zheng. Why was this deleted and left unrecorded? The answer is: All under Heaven has a fundamental boundary—that between the Yi peoples and the Xia. Was Jin not a state of ritual propriety and righteousness, and was Chu not a neighbor to birds and beasts? Although Duke Jing was weak, he still presided over the covenant of the Xia states. Zheng attached itself to Chu, fearing force rather than cherishing virtue, pursuing advantage rather than maintaining firm bonds of kinship. Its transformation for the worse had reached this extreme: how could Chu’s rescue merit praise? The commentary says: “Zheng possessed no goodness that deserved rescue; Chu could not gain the reputation of being able to rescue it.” Once this is understood, all under Heaven will recognize that the Yi are contemptible, and few will adopt their ways. When the Yi do not disrupt the Hua, is the fundamental boundary not firmly maintained? This shows that the sage’s recording and deletion were invariably undertaken with regard to rulers and ministers, Yi and Xia. How could the annals of individual states compare?

Yet what need is there to reproach Chu? How is Zheng even worth reproaching? Duke Jing of Jin inherited the hegemony, and the central states looked up to him. Should he not have used virtue and ritual propriety to draw back the estranged and win over those far away? Zheng allied with Chu but then promptly came to court: it had erred and repented. To seize its ruler, attack its state, and kill its envoy—what brutality! At Shaoling, Chu’s envoy was treated with ritual courtesy; at Xiaoyu, Zheng was trusted without suspicion. Duke Huan! Duke Dao! How much worthier they were than Duke Jing! Even so, Zhong and Zhi had ways of instructing them. Jing was neither Huan nor Dao, and his ministers were neither Zhong nor Zhi. How, then, could ritual propriety and trust be put into practice? Thus it is said: “The conduct of government depends upon the men.”

Book of Rites
“Thus the sage forms a triad with Heaven and Earth and stands alongside the ghosts and spirits, thereby conducting government.”
Liang Zuo

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
考試官訓導穆批〔見理精到而文足以發〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔講本天處興味自別〕
記者言聖人法造化以爲治以見治道之原也
蓋道之大原出於天也聖人法造化以爲治夫
豈私意臆度而爲之哉禮運承上章言政之意
以爲君者政之所自出也政者君之所由安也
能治其政以安其身舍聖人其誰與哉是故兩
儀奠而法象形道運於天地而不已也聖人則
仰觀俯察裁而成之以知其化育焉二氣行而
===
屈伸著事寓於鬼神而有迹也聖人則彰往察
來擬而議之以成其變化焉內蘊易簡之理而
覆載之功我其賛之參其兩而爲三矣中涵寂
感之幾而動靜之樞我其握之並其二而爲一
矣夫此豈有他哉凡以治吾之政而已蓋政莫
先於立教也體天地之撰而變通之則所以立
極而垂訓者資之愈深而教於是乎立矣政莫
要於定制也因鬼神之故而損益之則所以開
物而成務者循之可久而制於是乎定矣運用
punctuated:
考試官訓導穆批〔見理精到，而文足以發。〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔講本天處，興味自別。〕
記者言聖人法造化以爲治，以見治道之原也。蓋道之大原出於天也，聖人法造化以爲治，夫豈私意臆度而爲之哉？禮運承上章言政之意，以爲君者，政之所自出也；政者，君之所由安也。能治其政以安其身，舍聖人其誰與哉？是故兩儀奠而法象形，道運於天地而不已也。聖人則仰觀俯察，裁而成之，以知其化育焉。二氣行而屈伸著，事寓於鬼神而有迹也。聖人則彰往察來，擬而議之，以成其變化焉。內蘊易簡之理，而覆載之功，我其賛之，參其兩而爲三矣；中涵寂感之幾，而動靜之樞，我其握之，並其二而爲一矣。夫此豈有他哉？凡以治吾之政而已。蓋政莫先於立教也，體天地之撰而變通之，則所以立極而垂訓者，資之愈深，而教於是乎立矣。政莫要於定制也，因鬼神之故而損益之，則所以開物而成務者，循之可久，而制於是乎定矣。運用
translation_en:
Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor, comments: 〔The grasp of principle is penetrating and precise, and the writing fully expresses it.〕
Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: 〔The discussion of grounding government in Heaven has a distinctive richness of meaning.〕
The author of the Record says that the sage models his government on the creative transformations of nature, thereby revealing the source of the Way of government. For the great source of the Way issues from Heaven. When the sage models his government on nature’s creative transformations, how could he act upon private notions and conjecture? The “Evolution of Rites” chapter continues the preceding section’s discussion of government: the ruler is the source from which government proceeds, and government is the means by which the ruler secures his own peace. Who but a sage can order his government and thereby secure himself?
Thus, when the Two Powers, Heaven and Earth, are established and their patterns and images take form, the Way operates unceasingly within Heaven and Earth. The sage looks upward and examines what lies below, giving due measure and completion to their operations, so as to understand their transforming and nourishing work. When the two vital forces, yin and yang, circulate and their contraction and expansion become manifest, affairs lodge in the spirits and have perceptible traces. The sage makes the past manifest and examines what is to come, comparing and deliberating, so as to bring their transformations to completion.
Inwardly he possesses the principles of ease and simplicity. As for the work of sheltering and sustaining all things, he says, “I shall assist it,” joining Heaven and Earth as a third. Within him lie the subtle springs of stillness and response. As for the pivot of movement and rest, he says, “I shall grasp it,” uniting the two operations of the spirits into one. Could there be any other purpose in this? It is all simply to put his government in order.
In government, nothing takes precedence over establishing moral instruction. By embodying the workings of Heaven and Earth and adapting them to changing circumstances, the sage draws ever more deeply upon them to establish the supreme standard and leave teachings for posterity; moral instruction is thereby established. In government, nothing is more essential than determining institutions. By following the underlying workings of the spirits and making appropriate subtractions and additions, he provides a means of opening up the potential of things and bringing affairs to completion that can be followed enduringly; institutions are thereby determined. Putting these into practice…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
於一心推之萬變而皆宜所謂同民心而出治
道者此也建立於一時垂之萬世而無弊所謂
一道德而同風俗者此也夫然則政豈有不正
而身豈有不安者哉考之下文有曰君者立於
無過之地者也夫能正其身而無過則亦聖人
而已雖然記者之言蓋本於中庸也夫政卽三
重也無過卽寡過也參卽建之而不悖也並卽
質之而無疑也三代有道之長率由乎此後世
乃欲以區區智力把持天下毋怪乎其治之不
===
古若也噫
廉直勁正莊誠之音作而民肅敬
楊作舟
考試官訓導穆批不以金石絲竹入講蓋知音樂
之辨者
考試官教諭鄭批分析字義明白當是作者
記者審樂音之敬而知民心之敬焉夫音生於
心也心苟敬矣而其發之於音也寧不敬哉樂
記此章申言首章之意若謂心感於中而無常
punctuated:
於一心，推之萬變而皆宜，所謂同民心而出治道者，此也。建立於一時，垂之萬世而無弊，所謂一道德而同風俗者，此也。夫然則政豈有不正，而身豈有不安者哉？考之下文，有曰：「君者，立於無過之地者也。」夫能正其身而無過，則亦聖人而已。雖然，記者之言蓋本於《中庸》也。夫政卽三重也，無過卽寡過也，參卽建之而不悖也，並卽質之而無疑也。三代有道之長，率由乎此。後世乃欲以區區智力把持天下，毋怪乎其治之不古若也。噫！
廉直勁正莊誠之音作而民肅敬
楊作舟
考試官訓導穆批：「不以金石絲竹入講，蓋知音樂之辨者。」
考試官教諭鄭批：「分析字義明白，當是作者。」
記者審樂音之敬，而知民心之敬焉。夫音生於心也，心苟敬矣，而其發之於音也，寧不敬哉？《樂記》此章申言首章之意，若謂心感於中而無常
translation_en:
…within a single mind, and extended to the myriad changes, it is fitting in every case. This is what is meant by uniting the people’s hearts and bringing forth the way of government. Established in one age and handed down through ten thousand generations without ill effects: this is what is meant by unifying moral principles and bringing customs into accord. If this is so, how could government fail to be correct, or the ruler’s person fail to be secure? Examining the passage below, we find: “The ruler stands in a position free from error.” One who can rectify his own person and be without error must surely be a sage. Nevertheless, the recorder’s words are based on the Doctrine of the Mean. “Government” means the three weighty matters; “being without error” means having few errors; “forming a triad” means establishing things without contradiction; and “standing alongside” means testing things without doubt. The rulers of the Three Dynasties who possessed the Way all followed this. Later generations sought instead to hold the realm in their grasp through paltry cleverness and force. No wonder their government fell short of antiquity! Alas!
“When sounds of integrity, directness, firmness, uprightness, solemnity, and sincerity arise, the people become solemn and reverent.”
Yang Zuozhou
Comment by Examiner Mu, Assistant Instructor: “He does not bring bells, chime stones, strings, or pipes into his exposition. Evidently he understands the distinction between tones and music.”
Comment by Examiner Zheng, Instructor: “His analysis of the meanings of the words is clear. He must be an accomplished writer.”
The recorder examines the reverence in musical sounds and thereby knows the reverence in the people’s hearts. Sounds arise from the heart. If the heart is reverent, how could its expression in sound fail to be reverent? This chapter of the Record of Music elaborates the meaning of the opening chapter, as though saying that the heart is stirred within, with no fixed pattern…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
音發於外而有象然則音之作也豈惟喜怒可
知而已哉彼其應以生變稜隅整飭不混而淆
何其廉也變以成方節奏簡徑不句而曲何其
直也至剛至健抑之愈高無反無側守之愈確
又何其勁正乎恪恭祗愼不怠以荒純一敦固
不二而雜又何其莊誠乎倜然於永言之際而
有不可犯者存聽之者惕然而有所興也毅然
於咏歎之餘而有不可奪者在聞之者悚然而
知所勵也是音也果何從而生耶必其有所戒
也有嚴有翼而懍懍之是將有所畏也惟兢惟
一而惺惺之匪懈守之愈嚴而惰慢之心無自
而投則其音之不可犯也固也不然則姦而濫
矣寧不蕩然而忘返乎斂之愈約而非僻之心
無由而入則其音之不可奪也宜也不然則湎
而淫矣寧不薾然而莫振乎以是而觀則知音
之本於心也尚矣心不能敬而徒矯飾於聲音
之末以求其敬也胡可得哉抑又論之惟敬則
肅惟廉則勁而莊惟直則正而誠故曰其敬心
punctuated: 音發於外而有象。然則音之作也，豈惟喜怒可知而已哉？彼其應以生變，稜隅整飭，不混而淆，何其廉也！變以成方，節奏簡徑，不句而曲，何其直也！至剛至健，抑之愈高；無反無側，守之愈確，又何其勁正乎！恪恭祗愼，不怠以荒；純一敦固，不二而雜，又何其莊誠乎！倜然於永言之際，而有不可犯者存，聽之者惕然而有所興也；毅然於咏歎之餘，而有不可奪者在，聞之者悚然而知所勵也。是音也，果何從而生耶？必其有所戒也，有嚴有翼，而懍懍之是將；有所畏也，惟兢惟一，而惺惺之匪懈。守之愈嚴，而惰慢之心無自而投，則其音之不可犯也固也。不然，則姦而濫矣，寧不蕩然而忘返乎？斂之愈約，而非僻之心無由而入，則其音之不可奪也宜也。不然，則湎而淫矣，寧不薾然而莫振乎？以是而觀，則知音之本於心也尚矣。心不能敬，而徒矯飾於聲音之末，以求其敬也，胡可得哉？抑又論之，惟敬則肅，惟廉則勁而莊，惟直則正而誠。故曰：「其敬心
translation_en: …sound issues outward and takes perceptible form. Thus, when sound arises, can it reveal only joy and anger? As its responses produce variations, its contours are well ordered, neither confused nor muddled: how distinct and disciplined it is! As its variations form patterns, its rhythms are simple and direct, neither winding nor crooked: how straight it is! Utterly firm and vigorous, the more it is pressed down, the higher it rises; neither turning back nor inclining aside, the more firmly it is maintained, the more steadfast it becomes. How forceful and upright it is! Respectful, reverent, and cautious, it does not lapse into indolence and neglect; single-minded, sincere, and firm, it is neither divided nor mixed. How solemn and sincere it is! Amid the sustained singing, it stands loftily apart, possessing something that cannot be affronted; those who listen are stirred to alertness and inspired. Beyond the chanting and sighing, it remains resolute, possessing something that cannot be wrested away; those who hear are awed and know to exert themselves. From what, indeed, does such sound arise? Surely those who produce it have something against which they guard: solemn and circumspect, they sustain their trembling vigilance. They have something they hold in awe: cautious and single-minded, they remain watchful without relaxing. The stricter their self-restraint, the less opportunity idle and negligent thoughts have to insinuate themselves; it is therefore natural that their sound cannot be affronted. Otherwise it would become corrupt and unrestrained: would it not wander unchecked and forget to return? The more closely they gather themselves inward, the less opportunity wrongful and perverse thoughts have to enter; it is therefore fitting that their sound cannot be deflected. Otherwise it would become besotted and excessive: would it not sink into lassitude and fail to recover? Viewed in this way, sound’s foundation in the heart is indeed fundamental. If the heart cannot be reverent, how could one attain reverence merely by artificially embellishing its outward expression in sound? To pursue the argument further: reverence brings solemnity; distinctness and discipline bring strength and gravity; straightness brings uprightness and sincerity. Thus it is said: “When their reverent hearts…”

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
感者其聲直以廉義巳盡矣然民心之所以敬
者則又在先王德澤入之之深而禮義養之之
固也故曰先王慎所以感之者
第貳場
論
先王守禮樂之本
馬應義
同考試官教諭沈批〔前輩謂作論如文與可畫竹觀子殆胸中有全竹者真士中不多得也首選允宜〕
===
考試官訓導穆批〔法度嚴密意味深長殆探本之論也可敬可服〕
考試官教諭鄭批〔文勢若長江大河文彩若奇葩麗卉低頭東野之拜將不敢抗顏於子矣〕
論曰聖人之爲斯世也天而巳矣夫苟至於天
焉吾知藏於人心之微而不在於耳目觀瞻之
頃關於天地之大而不假於器數聲容之末是
則無體無聲者也萬一聖人於此弗以天處之
而以人御之强握而矯拂暌疑而乖違則萬轍
punctuated:
感者，其聲直以廉」，義巳盡矣。然民心之所以敬者，則又在先王德澤入之之深，而禮義養之之固也。故曰：「先王慎所以感之者。」

第貳場

論

先王守禮樂之本

馬應義

同考試官教諭沈批〔前輩謂作論如文與可畫竹，觀子殆胸中有全竹者，真士中不多得也，首選允宜。〕

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
千岐爭馳競逐人者勝而天者微矣聖人與天
同運者也而肯以人勝天耶唐之太宗何如主
也而遽謂治之隆替不關於禮樂焉是人矣而
非天也先王守禮樂之本宋儒司馬光殆懼夫
後世之昧者弗察焉而覺之也請終言之禮云
而不以玉帛樂云而不以鍾鼓孔子之言也禮
所以節文乎仁義樂所以樂乎仁義孟子之言
也知孔孟論禮樂之旨則知司馬氏探先王禮
樂之本矣夷攷其時衣裳宮室之制作樂崇德
===
之旨固聞諸易也而說焉未詳所謂禮樂者猶
夫太始之天也伯夷寅清之言后夔直温之教
固聞諸書也而語焉未竟所謂禮樂者猶夫太
初之天也噫不灼其影昧者弗見也不烈其聲
聵者弗聞也聖人於此將聽其岐轍之紛紜騰
口之靡定哉聖人要亦有變通宜民之術矣於
是以開闢天地之規模而極夫世變江河之思
慮亦惟因夫民心固有之禮而示之以禮禮一
順也天也順之外固無禮矣因人心固有之樂
punctuated:
千岐，爭馳競逐，人者勝而天者微矣。聖人與天同運者也，而肯以人勝天耶？唐之太宗何如主也，而遽謂治之隆替不關於禮樂焉？是人矣，而非天也。先王守禮樂之本，宋儒司馬光殆懼夫後世之昧者弗察焉而覺之也。

請終言之。禮云而不以玉帛，樂云而不以鍾鼓，孔子之言也。禮所以節文乎仁義，樂所以樂乎仁義，孟子之言也。知孔孟論禮樂之旨，則知司馬氏探先王禮樂之本矣。夷攷其時，衣裳宮室之制、作樂崇德之旨，固聞諸《易》也，而說焉未詳，所謂禮樂者猶夫太始之天也。伯夷寅清之言、后夔直温之教，固聞諸《書》也，而語焉未竟，所謂禮樂者猶夫太初之天也。

噫！不灼其影，昧者弗見也；不烈其聲，聵者弗聞也。聖人於此，將聽其岐轍之紛紜、騰口之靡定哉？聖人要亦有變通宜民之術矣。於是以開闢天地之規模，而極夫世變江河之思慮，亦惟因夫民心固有之禮而示之以禮。禮，一順也，天也；順之外，固無禮矣。因人心固有之樂
translation_en:
…a thousand diverging paths, racing and competing with one another: the human prevails, while the heavenly grows faint. The sage moves in concert with Heaven; would he willingly let the human overcome the heavenly? What sort of ruler was Emperor Taizong of the Tang, that he should so readily declare that the flourishing or decline of government had no connection with rites and music? This is human, not heavenly. The former kings preserved the foundation of rites and music. Sima Guang, the Song Confucian scholar, presumably feared that the unenlightened of later ages would fail to perceive this, and sought to awaken them to it.

Allow me to complete the argument. To speak of rites without meaning merely jade and silk, and of music without meaning merely bells and drums—these are the words of Confucius. Rites give measured expression to benevolence and righteousness; music gives joy in benevolence and righteousness—these are the words of Mencius. If one understands the purport of Confucius’s and Mencius’s discussions of rites and music, one understands how Sima Guang investigated their foundation under the former kings. On calmly examining those times, we find that the institutions of clothing and dwellings, and the purpose of making music to exalt virtue, are indeed known from the Book of Changes. Yet its explanations are not detailed: what it calls rites and music still resemble Heaven at the primordial beginning. Bo Yi’s words concerning reverence and purity, and Hou Kui’s teaching concerning uprightness and gentleness, are indeed known from the Book of Documents. Yet its account is not exhaustive: what it calls rites and music still resemble Heaven at the first inception.

Alas! Unless its image is made bright, the benighted cannot see it; unless its sound is made forceful, the deaf cannot hear it. Would the sage, confronted with this, simply allow a confusion of divergent paths and an incessant clamor of conflicting voices? The sage surely also possesses methods of adapting to circumstances for the people’s benefit. Thus, with a scope befitting the opening of Heaven and Earth, he exhaustively considers the changes of the world as they flow like rivers [?]. He simply draws upon the rites inherent in the people’s hearts and makes them manifest through ritual observances. Rites are wholly accord; they are Heaven. Beyond accord, there are indeed no rites. Drawing upon the music inherent in the human heart…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
而示之以樂樂一和也天也和之外固無樂矣
於戲禮焉而示之以禮之天樂焉而示之以樂
之天聖人無廼斲天下之朴而不欲遊於堯舜
民相忘之天歟殆不然遭適至之時神化裁之
妙雲興波動而清明不移朴分質剖而渾厚猶
在所謂無體無聲而人心之天者固自若也故
曰聖人之爲斯世也天而已矣夫以人道之大
經而維持人文之脉絡而接續吾聖人爲禮樂
計也蓋已悉矣而議禮樂者往往築室而聚訟
===
何哉良有由矣蓋自夫比屋可封之俗弗見焉
而後世談禮者始索之文爲之末自夫康衢詩
歌之詠弗聞焉而後世議樂者始求之形器之
粗是則外矣而非內迹矣而非化尚安能囿一
世民物於至順至和之天歟知乎此則知先王
所以敎禮樂者悉原於天也天者何觀諸其道
而已天不變道亦不變一氣之相爲流通自太
極而來至於今不易也日月之在天至於今明
也江河之在地至於今流也山嶽至於今峙草
punctuated:
而示之以樂。樂，一和也，天也；和之外，固無樂矣。於戲！禮焉而示之以禮之天，樂焉而示之以樂之天，聖人無廼斲天下之朴，而不欲遊於堯舜民相忘之天歟？殆不然。遭適至之時，神化裁之妙，雲興波動而清明不移，朴分質剖而渾厚猶在，所謂無體無聲而人心之天者，固自若也。故曰：「聖人之爲斯世也，天而已矣。」夫以人道之大經而維持，人文之脉絡而接續，吾聖人爲禮樂計也，蓋已悉矣。而議禮樂者往往築室而聚訟，何哉？良有由矣。蓋自夫比屋可封之俗弗見焉，而後世談禮者始索之文爲之末；自夫康衢詩歌之詠弗聞焉，而後世議樂者始求之形器之粗。是則外矣而非內，迹矣而非化，尚安能囿一世民物於至順至和之天歟？知乎此，則知先王所以敎禮樂者悉原於天也。
天者何？觀諸其道而已。天不變，道亦不變。一氣之相爲流通，自太極而來，至於今不易也。日月之在天，至於今明也；江河之在地，至於今流也；山嶽至於今峙，草
translation_en:
…and shows them music. Music is simply harmony; it is Heaven. Outside harmony, there can indeed be no music. Ah! In ritual, he shows them the Heaven inherent in ritual; in music, he shows them the Heaven inherent in music. Could it be that the sage hews away the uncarved simplicity of the world and does not wish to dwell in that natural realm where Yao and Shun and their people were oblivious of one another? Surely not. Meeting the needs of the moment, he brings wondrous spiritual efficacy to the work of transformation and regulation. Clouds rise and waves stir, yet clarity remains unchanged; the uncarved block is divided and its substance cut apart, yet its unaffected integrity remains. What is called the formless and soundless Heaven within the human heart remains just as it was. Thus it is said: “What the sage does for this world is simply Heaven.” By sustaining the great guiding principles of the human way and continuing the vital threads of human culture, our sage has surely considered ritual and music in their entirety. Yet those who debate ritual and music often resemble people building a house who gather conflicting opinions. Why is this? There is indeed a reason. Once the customs under which every household had someone worthy of enfeoffment were no longer seen, later generations discussing ritual began to seek it in the superficial details of formal observances. Once the songs sung along the broad thoroughfares were no longer heard, later generations discussing music began to seek it in the crude externals of physical forms and instruments. These are outward things, not inward ones; traces, not transforming influence. How could they possibly encompass all the people and things of an age within Heaven’s perfect accord and perfect harmony? Understanding this, one understands that the former kings’ teaching of ritual and music originated entirely in Heaven.
What is Heaven? One need only observe its Way. Heaven does not change, and neither does the Way. The single vital energy circulates everywhere; from the Great Ultimate down to the present, this has not changed. The sun and moon in the heavens shine to this day; the rivers upon the earth flow to this day; the mountains stand to this day; the grasses…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
木禽獸蟲魚至於今蕃且育也凡若此者非有
度數焉而成禮非有均節焉而成樂所謂不言
而化無爲而成者也兹其所謂無體之禮無聲
之樂也而道實爲之故曰天也夫天也其孰能
知之曰唯聖人能知之其孰能體之曰唯聖人
能體之何也禮也者人心之禮即人心之天也
樂也者人心之樂亦人心之天也由是聖人因
其天者而教禮樂焉叙爲彝倫脩爲人紀置之
充然大順之域夏籥之用殷輅之乘周冕之服
===
不與焉洽爲德澤流爲雅頌納於藹然至和之
中大夏之興大濩之作大武之奏不與焉當時
所謂禮樂者惟見其四極和寧而已惟見其萬
民咸悅而已惟見其江漢無犯而已尊其尊親
其親而辭遜於天高地下之間兹無體之禮也
聲相應氣相求而舞蹈於蟲鳴螽躍之地兹無
聲之樂也論至於斯則知聖人之心大乎天地
不足爲容皦乎日月不足爲明嵬乎泰華不足
爲高渾乎江河不足爲流轉知之者天也同之
punctuated: 木禽獸蟲魚至於今蕃且育也。凡若此者，非有度數焉而成禮，非有均節焉而成樂，所謂不言而化、無爲而成者也。兹其所謂無體之禮、無聲之樂也，而道實爲之，故曰天也。夫天也，其孰能知之？曰：唯聖人能知之。其孰能體之？曰：唯聖人能體之。何也？禮也者，人心之禮，即人心之天也；樂也者，人心之樂，亦人心之天也。由是聖人因其天者而教禮樂焉，叙爲彝倫，脩爲人紀，置之充然大順之域，夏籥之用、殷輅之乘、周冕之服不與焉；洽爲德澤，流爲雅頌，納於藹然至和之中，大夏之興、大濩之作、大武之奏不與焉。當時所謂禮樂者，惟見其四極和寧而已，惟見其萬民咸悅而已，惟見其江漢無犯而已。尊其尊，親其親，而辭遜於天高地下之間，兹無體之禮也；聲相應，氣相求，而舞蹈於蟲鳴螽躍之地，兹無聲之樂也。論至於斯，則知聖人之心，大乎天地不足爲容，皦乎日月不足爲明，嵬乎泰華不足爲高，渾乎江河不足爲流轉。知之者天也，同之
translation_en:
…trees, birds, beasts, insects, and fish continue to multiply and flourish to this day. In all such things, ritual takes shape without prescribed measures, and music takes shape without regulated rhythms. This is what is meant by transforming without speaking and accomplishing without acting. Here is what is called ritual without bodily form and music without sound. It is truly the Way that brings these about; hence we call it Heaven.

Who can understand Heaven? The answer is: only the sage can understand it. Who can embody it? The answer is: only the sage can embody it. Why? Ritual is the ritual inherent in the human heart—that is, the Heaven within the human heart. Music is the music inherent in the human heart, and it too is the Heaven within the human heart. Thus the sage teaches ritual and music on the basis of this Heaven within. He orders them into the enduring human relationships and cultivates them into the guiding principles of human life, placing people in a realm fully possessed of great concord. The use of Xia flutes, riding in Yin carriages, and wearing Zhou ceremonial caps have no part in this. He spreads them as beneficent virtue and lets them flow forth as Elegantiae and Hymns, bringing people into an abundant state of perfect harmony. The mounting of the Great Xia dance, the performance of the Great Huo dance, and the playing of the Great Wu dance music have no part in this.

What was then called ritual and music was manifest simply in peace and harmony throughout the four extremities, in the joy of all the people, and in the absence of transgression in the lands of the Jiang and Han rivers. To honor those whom one should honor, cherish those whom one should cherish, and act with deference and humility between lofty Heaven and lowly Earth: this is ritual without bodily form. Sounds answering one another, vital breaths seeking their kind, and dancing amid chirping insects and leaping grasshoppers: this is music without sound.

Pursuing the discussion thus far, we understand that the sage’s heart is so vast that Heaven and Earth cannot contain it; so radiant that the sun and moon cannot match its brightness; so lofty that Mount Tai and Mount Hua cannot match its height; and so boundless that the Jiang and Yellow rivers cannot match its ceaseless flow. What understands it is Heaven; what is one with it…

title: 嘉靖十六年雲南鄉試錄
text:
者道也化之者人也漸而澤之者天下後世也
天也聖人也不可以差殊觀也故曰天也奚俟
求諸旦暮之功索諸形器之末哉抑嘗因光之
慨夫唐而考夫唐之禮樂矣蓋自貞觀垂統內
有慚德而閨門之禮樂紊矣顯慶多中决之政
而朝廷之禮樂廢矣一傳而有斜封墨勅之濫
再傳而有漁陽召亂之釁又再傳而有閹宦擅
政之禍上下李唐諸君所謂垂統弗正而繼體
昏風將倂其本而仆之人矣而非天也烏足以
===
言禮樂哉是無怪乎司馬氏憂深思遠而爲中
正和平之論以開夫時君世主之天也有子曰
君子務本曾子曰此謂知本愚於光禮樂之言
亦云是爲論
表

劉舉良
同考試官教諭沈批麗而能則冲淡可喜
punctuated:
者道也，化之者人也，漸而澤之者天下後世也。天也，聖人也，不可以差殊觀也，故曰天也。奚俟求諸旦暮之功，索諸形器之末哉？抑嘗因光之慨夫唐，而考夫唐之禮樂矣。蓋自貞觀垂統，內有慚德，而閨門之禮樂紊矣；顯慶多中决之政，而朝廷之禮樂廢矣。一傳而有斜封墨勅之濫，再傳而有漁陽召亂之釁，又再傳而有閹宦擅政之禍。上下李唐諸君，所謂垂統弗正，而繼體昏，風將倂其本而仆之。人矣，而非天也，烏足以言禮樂哉？是無怪乎司馬氏憂深思遠，而爲中正和平之論，以開夫時君世主之天也。有子曰：「君子務本。」曾子曰：「此謂知本。」愚於光禮樂之言亦云是。爲論。
表
擬宋輔臣謝賜御製瑞聖園觀稼城南觀麥詩表。祥符九年。
劉舉良
同考試官教諭沈批：「麗而能則，冲淡可喜。」
translation_en:
